speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to the five questions listed on the order paper is as follows: All dealings in radioactive materials, including radioactive wastes, are and have been since 1947 controlled by the atomic energy control board, through
regulations made under the Atomic Energy Control Act, and a licensing system established under the regulations. The current regulations are the atomic energy control regulations approved by order in council P.C. 1960/-348 of March 17, 1960.
All persons handling or disposing of radioactive materials are required under section 402 of the regulations to take all reasonable and proper precautions to prevent injury or damage to persons or property and are required by part VI of the regulations to ensure that no person is exposed to radiation in excess of specified amounts. Applicants for licences to obtain radioactive isotopes are required to specify the manner in which waste is to be disposed of, and the board or inspection officers may specify additional precautions. Permits issued by the board authorizing the working of deposits of radioactive minerals require the operators to comply with provincial or territorial requirements as to mine, safety and cognate matters, as well as with the board's regulations.
Inspection to ensure compliance is normally carried out through the Department of National Health and Welfare or provincial health authorities or, in the case of mining operations, by the appropriate provincial authorities. The board retains its over-all rights of inspection and direction. In view of its great experience and competence in the field, Atomic Energy of Canada has been made responsible for ensuring that its own operations comply with the regulations.
Under the act, section 20, proceedings in case of infraction may be taken by either federal or provincial authorities.

1.	Have standards governing the manner in which radioactive wastes should be disposed of been set or suggested by any United Nations agency or international authority?
2.	If so, (a) by what agency; (b) when; (c) what are they; (d) what position has been taken by the Canadian government?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STANDARDS GOVERNING DISPOSAL OF RADIOACTIVE WASTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the request of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, I have been asked to reply to this question.
1.	Yes, as regards the disposal of radioactive waste into the sea.
2.	(a) By the United Nations conference on the law of the sea. By the ad hoc panel on

Starred Questions
radioactive waste disposal into the sea appointed by the international atomic energy agency.
(b)	In 1958 and in February, 1960.
(c)	Article 25 of the convention on the high seas adopted by the 1958 United Nations conference on the law of the sea at Geneva, which is not yet in force, contains the following general provisions:
1.	Every state shall take measures to prevent pollution of the seas from the dumping of radioactive waste, taking into account any standards and regulations which may be formulated by the competent international organizations.
2.	All states shall co-operate with the competent international organizations in taking measures for the prevention of pollution of the seas or air space above, resulting from any activities with radioactive materials or other harmful agents.
Then follows some technical information, Mr. Speaker.
The report of the ad hoc panel on radioactive waste disposal into the sea of the international atomic energy agency contains recommendations which are at present under study by member governments and the details of which have consequently not yet been made public. In general they are that though highly radioactive wastes should not be disposed of into the sea, sufficiently safe control can be maintained for wastes of low or intermediate activity. The panel recommends that the exposure limits stated in the most recent recommendation of the international commission on radiological protection be followed as a guide to safe disposal and that disposal sites should be designated by the responsible national or international authority, monitored regularly and a registry kept of all disposals.
(d)	As to the position taken by the Canadian government, Canada supported article 25 both in committee and in plenary session of the 1958 conference and has signed the convention.
The recommendations made by the ad hoc panel are at present under study by the appropriate departments with a view to formulating the Canadian position.

Yesterday the hon. member for Assiniboia asked me this question, which was a continuation of an earlier question:
Has the Prime Minister any report to make on the meeting on June 8 with the London railroad workers' council which dealt with the transfer of C.N.R. passenger car repair work from the London shops, at which meeting the Prime Minister presided?
As the hon. member knows, under the law as it stands the minister is prohibited from interfering in any way in the decisions of management with regard to the day to day operation of the railway. That prohibition applies to all members of the government. The decision in so far as this transfer of work from London is concerned was made by the railway company. However, following the discussions and the representations made by a committee of the London railroad workers' council, presided over by Mr. Clifford M. Phillips, the railway company had indicated

that for the purpose of ascertaining the situation, various courses of action were explored by the railroad management.
One suggestion made was that the question be referred to the royal commission on transportation for its consideration. However, in the opinion of that body a matter of this kind did not come within the ambit of the terms of reference or scope of authority of the commission. Subsequently the president of the Canadian National Railways announced that it would not consider it advisable in the interest of the railway to alter the decision to transfer the passenger car repair work from the London shops. However, at the same time he made it clear that the Canadian National Railways was planning to set up new administrative regional headquarters in London as part of its general plan for decentralization.

I feel most keenly the position of many of the employees who, after many years of service, find themselves unable to continue in their vocation, and I will have the government give consideration to the amendment of the powers of the royal commission in order to cover this full situation arising from automation and otherwise.

41. Grant in respect of the net operating requirements of the radio and television services. $62,085,000.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to bring up a small point arising out of the remarks made on July 8 by the hon. member for Vancouver South, who I believe has left a wrong impression with the committee on this matter. I refer hon. gentlemen to the remarks of the hon. member as found at page 6012 of Hansard of July 8, where he said:
The argument seems to have been that any money spent on outlets in big cities is wasted because it has not been spent in bringing the benefits of the C.B.C. to remote areas ... It is just as important to promote Canadianism in the cities, and considering that most of our new Canadians flock to the cities it is perhaps a little more important than it is to bring entertainment and the Canadian viewpoint to remote areas.
We have had C.B.C. programs available to the cities and some of the urban centres for many years. I know myself we have been able to receive C.B.C. programs for over 15 years; also in the cities they have the choice of several stations. They are able to pick up radio stations and television stations, and in some instances they are now requesting the inauguration of colour television. At the same time we are not giving even the benefits of radio to some of our rural areas.
We are not asking the C.B.C. to undertake heavy expenditures. They are doing a good job in their endeavour to put on worth-while programs. All we are asking for is the installation of a low frequency booster station to bring in C.B.C. programs so that the people in the rural areas may be able to receive them. In the vicinity of the Rocky mountains, as I mentioned the other day, we have very sporadic reception, especially in the lake Windermere valley in Kootenay East. In some places we are not able to get a C.B.C. production of any kind. I bring this matter up because it relates to the matter raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South. I believe this is one matter which should receive the serious consideration of the department.
Supply-C.B.C.

Mr. Chairman, the last speaker raised a point which is of considerable concern to many of us. The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek dealt with his situation; mine is comparable. We both have low voltage stations with restricted areas of listening, and it does seem to me, sir, that out of its budget the C.B.C. might very well give consideration to the establishment of boosters in order that audiences may be enlarged.
One hears a great deal concerning the C.B.C. It is condemned; it is not praised too often. I am not particularly a television addict but I do think perhaps we often overlook the fact that there are certain programs -I am referring now particularly to "Farm Forum", "Citizens' Forum", "Close-Up" and "Viewpoint", and programs of that kind- which give the Canadian people a view of their country and of its potential that could be gained in no other way. I do say there is an opportunity for the C.B.C. by means of boosters to greatly enlarge its audiences. There is an opportunity to bring before more Canadians the good work the C.B.C., is doing.

Mr. Chairman, I want to make a few brief remarks. Possibly this matter might have been more properly discussed under item 42. However, for various reasons I was not able to speak on that item, and I should like to make my remarks now. They have to do with the consolidation of the existing facilities that C.B.C. and CBUT have in Vancouver. On March 23 of last year I asked the Minister of National Revenue, the following question, as reported at page 2140 of Hansard:
As the minister is doubtless aware, the C.B.C. radio and T.V. studios in Vancouver are at present situated in three different locations. With a view to increasing administrative efficiency and reducing production costs, as well as to create employment, would the minister advise whether the C.B.C. has given, or will give, consideration to the erection in Vancouver of a building which would house all the radio and T.V. facilities of the C.B.C.?
A statement was made before the parliamentary committee on broadcasting last year by Mr. Bushnell, and he concluded that statement by saying:
In addition, we ourselves face a number of capital projects which must be undertaken if we are to achieve our goal of maximum efficiency at minimum cost to the Canadian taxpayer; probably an example of this is the importance of consolidating our production facilities in the large centres of Montreal and Toronto where we are now too widely dispersed.
No mention is made of Vancouver. I understand that Vancouver is one of the originating stations of the C.B.C., and certainly we have marvellous facilities to make that city a consolidated production centre. I say this in view of the fact that I am led to believe we

Supply-C.B.C.
pay $80,000 a year on rental facilities alone for the three separate locations. Over a period of five years it would come to almost half a million dollars. This has been going on for some time now. I would seriously urge the minister to make representations to the department so that an early start may be made on a single building. We own, as I understand it, the property on which the CBUT stations are located on Georgia street, which is a substantial piece of property. I see no reason why we cannot get started on a building at this time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am of the opinion that not enough work has been done by the department in the field of experimentation in developing transmitters, and particularly small transmitters, which would work off the microwave set-up that we now have and supply coverage to places at least within 100 miles of the microwave tower. I am thinking of the small repeater stations such as we use for radio itself, where you put in a radio transmitter of very low voltage that has a radius of 25 miles and goes on and off automatically with the station that it is following. We hear continually that the Japanese, for instance, have developed a very low cost radio transmitter which would work on our microwave set-up. If this is so, I would think that the C.B.C. itself could do some planning for the development of a similar type of device. It would be economical to install this type of device, even disregarding the advertising potentiality and the things that would be necessary if a small station were to be put in by private enterprise.
In many communities, particularly in northern Ontario, there is a fringe area which could be supplied with radio reception if there was a much more economical method of getting transmission to those areas. Some of those communities have gone to the expense of erecting towers on a community basis and using coaxial cable. In most instances this has proved unsatisfactory. In some instances, and this is true of my own area, a private station has put in satellites which are quite effective and are doing a fairly good job but, Mr. Chairman, these all produce one bad result. It is true that the areas may be too small to finance their own studios and their own set-ups, but it seems to me we lose a great deal when we combine a very large area and feed to it the type of coverage that would be satisfactory in one of the main centres of that area rather than the outside points. This means that the people in the fringe areas served by satellites, while they do get television reception, get very little in the programs that is of a local nature.

It is impossible for the companies themselves to rectify this because the cost of equipment for mobile transmission is very high. This, of course, is the major objection to putting in a repeater type satellite which works only off the microwave. There is no opportunity for local broadcasting. There is no local programming at all; therefore this type of station should be used mainly in those areas where there is going to be no opportunity now or in the foreseeable future for the people to get local coverage from television stations in their own areas.
I should like to refer also to the operations of the C.B.C. in the field of programming. I certainly am not a long-hair, and I do not particularly care for that type of program. I have been struck, and I think perhaps the minister has too, by the reception given the program from down east, the Don Messer show. I understand that the C.B.C. was shocked to find it had a high rating. It was put on as a substitute program, and now they find it is one of the most popular programs on the C.B.C.
It seems to me that while we need culture, it does not have to be of the long-hair type. We do not have to carry a violin under our arm nor do we have to grow a beard to appreciate music. Some of us like the type of music to which we can listen while doing our work. At the same time we do not have to sit down and emit some of the sounds which come from some of the professional types who are interested in good music.
I feel that in so far as these Wednesday night radio programs are concerned, sometimes without a doubt we have put on the most stupid type of program possible. From listening to these programs it would appear that the C.B.C. gets a good three-act play, but then only has enough time and money to put on the middle act. You never know where the play begins or ends. You often wonder if the announcer is going to say that this will be continued the next Wednesday night.
Perhaps this type of play appeals to some people, but it is not necessarily what we should consider to be Canadian culture. We should develop a more homey type of culture which would appeal to the east, to the west, and to the north. We could have some programs of the other type for Toronto and some of the other beatnik cities. I am not suggesting we should eliminate them, but we should attempt to strike some balance so we would have programs that appeal to all Canadians rather than a situation which results in Wednesday night radio listening being pretty well eliminated for a large number of Canadians.

We should like also to commend the C.B.C. on the high calibre of many of the programs. It is my opinion that the C.B.C. does a better job on the commentary programs than do the United States stations. It seems to me the commentators are less biased and more interested in giving three, four or five sides of an argument than they are in admitting that there may be only two. A great deal of our programming of that nature is very constructive and very well done.
Recently, Mr. Chairman, a problem developed in connection with one of the programs that I consider is making an exceptional contribution to Canada. I refer to the program "Close-Up". I was shocked when I heard the minister say he would give Mr. Roberts, the attorney general of Ontario, the right to ascertain who the people were who were involved in this particular program in which the attorney general was interested.
First, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that I have known Mr. Roberts for many years. He originally practised law in my area. I was surprised, indeed, to find him saying that he did not know these things were going on because he had never known about them during his practice of law. Well, this may be lawyers' talk, but it certainly does not make much sense. I know Mr. Roberts had a general practice in my area, and the people of my area are no different from people in other places. The cases which he handled must have contained the same ingredients as the cases that were handled in other places.
In my opinion the girl who appeared on "Close-Up" did a very good job. I could not care less if she was lying the first time or if she is lying now. What she said about the divorce situation in Canada was true then and it is true now, whether it affected her or whether it affected the general public. We all know that at least the ingredients in that broadcast were true. Everyone knows it. When some of these leading lawyers say they did not know about this, in my opinion that is just so much eyewash.
I think this young lady was put in a very embarrassing position when it was suggested that she should tell her story to the attorney general of Ontario. There were many complications in this situation. First, she had to protect the C.B.C. people with whom she was dealing, if at all possible, and she also had to protect the other people with whom she was dealing, who in that case would be the legal profession. It seemed to me that many lawyers in Ontario would have been involved and would have faced probable disbarment if Mr. Roberts could have got the testimony from her which the newspaper stories I read suggested that he wanted.
Supply-C.B.C.
I think, Mr. Chairman, we are doing a job in Canada. We are presenting on the C.B.C., as we should, all sides of various arguments. I am sure that we have to protect those people whom we ask to participate in these broadcasts. We have to protect, as well, the people who work in the industry. I believe we hire these people on the understanding that they have some ability, that they are not completely new to the field. Certain precautions should be taken, and perhaps these should be more closely regulated.
However, every newspaperman with whom I have talked is very familiar with the libel laws, very familiar with what he can and cannot do. Most of the newspapers insist on this before they allow anybody to write a story. The C.B.C. have probably taken the same precautions. If they have, then I think they should take all precautions possible to ensure that those whom they ask to participate in broadcasts are protected. I would make a personal guess that the honesty of the broadcast in question was much greater than the honesty that has appeared since the investigation took place.
I am only saying that if we are going to ask people to put forth their views, we should give them an assurance that they can be protected. We should take all the precautions necessary to make sure that they are protected. I have listened to many controversial subjects discussed on these broadcasts. I have talked with a large number of people, not people in the long-hair class but people who are interested in getting more information on Canadian topics, and they have been very pleased with the presentations made on "Close-Up" as well as some of the other programs on the C.B.C.
I think it is safe to say, Mr. Chairman, that the Canadian people have been more interested in the controversial type of program than they have been in many of the other programs that have been carried. It seems to me that we should not devote our programming to what would satisfy one group of people or what would satisfy another group of people, but should attempt to develop a well-rounded series of programs. There should be heavy music for those who like it, but I think it should be in proportion to the number of those who like it. There should be some jazz music, but that also should be in proportion to the number who would appreciate it. The programs in the middle group should be, in the main, the type of programs that will tend to develop Canadianism and the things that separate us from our neighbours in the United States.
If we do not do this; if the main part of our programming is only a reproduction of that which satisfies United States audiences,

Supply-C.B.C.
we are going to have great difficulty in establishing in Canada any type of nationalism at all. It would appear that this should be one of the functions and indeed one of the fundamental functions of the C.B.C., so that we can develop in Canada a Canadian culture and a Canadian outlook and give a Canadian expression which will be a little bit different. I suggest that many of the things that are considered suitable by some of the people in charge of programming have not, in my opinion, tended to the middle but have been rather on the extreme.
I believe that the C.B.C., in the main, has done a very good job. If it had not been for the C.B.C. I am quite sure that my local station, which is a privately owned one, would be broadcasting more soap dramas and more advertising of all kinds. I am quite sure it would have been advertising indiscriminately if it had not had the competition that it has had for many years from the C.B.C. The C.B.C. itself is able to develop a standard and to produce to that standard in the major cities, something which again is carried over into private broadcasting.
I think it has done a good job. We have had differences of opinion with it and probably we shall continue to do so. However, in the main I think it is making a contribution. As it grows older it also will grow up and will concentrate much more on what would be truly Canadianism, something which is not an extreme at either one end of the cultural ladder or the other but which would satisfy many of us who are just in the middle and who understand and appreciate good music or fair music. This concentration in turn will tend to develop more of a Canadianism than will some of the things that have been done, and I refer particularly to Wednesday night C.B.C.

I am rising just to make two comments on the speech we have just heard from the hon. member for Timiskaming. My first comment is that I also, like the hon. member, on the whole approve of the C.B.C. and have done so over the years. I too think that on balance they have done a very good job indeed. I have some criticisms and I will have more. However, I would not like my criticisms to alter that fact.
The other comment is that I was rather astonished at some of the arguments of the hon. gentleman. It seems to me that if the C.B.C. would be careful not to put on its programs people who need protection from the police, they would not get into any trouble in the first place. It seems to me that we do not vote money here for the purpose of having persons do broadcasts for the

purpose of confessing that they have committed crimes for which they could be charged in the courts. I think the C.B.C. made a great error in judgment, and I hope that in future they will not put on their programs unconvicted burglars, murderers, thieves or perjurers boasting about their crimes. It seems to me that there are in this country enough people who are capable of entertaining and instructing the Canadian people without portraying confessed but unconvicted criminals.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Before the hon. member sits down, may I ask him a question?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Would he not consider that this type of program is something along the line of the activities of those newspaper reporters who over the years have, on occasion, made contact with someone who may be outside of the law or who is considered at the time to be outside of the law, and have carried on interviews which were published in their newspapers and tend to make a change in the status quo? In many cases murderers have given themselves up to newspaper reporters. Would the hon. member not agree that this type of program is somewhat in the same category?

I certainly do not agree with anything of the sort. I do not think a newspaper reporter or anyone else has any right to shield self-confessed criminals from the police. It is the duty of every member of the public to report to the police any evidence he has of any crime. If we are to have any organized society at all, that duty must be upheld. If we want to change the divorce laws that is an entirely different matter, but so long as the law is the law it should be obeyed. No one who admits to having committed a crime should be shielded from the rigours of the law merely because that person has in addition made an exhibition of himself.

As an illustration, Mr. Chairman, I would say that in the evening news, considerable importance is attached to events in Cuba,

Indonesia, Ceylon or elsewhere, and that little time is left for news from Ottawa.
The people of Canada should take an interest in their own politics. They should know what is happening in Ottawa. They have a right xo know what their representatives are doing in the House of Commons.

In the second place, Mr. Chairman, I should like to associate myself with the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Tremblay) in expressing my appreciation to the C.B.C. for the quality of some of its programs, which really show good taste and are genuinely useful.

It is not as easy for us, as it seems to be for the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard), to have the run of the C.B.C. building to see what is going on. Therefore, I support the suggestion made in this house that a royal commission be established. It would be of benefit both to the C.B.C. and to the people of Canada.
This suggestion should be accepted because any member who rises in this house is impelled by a sense of duty. At times, the points he raises may be debatable, but he should not be accused of partisanship and his interventions should not be considered as mud-slinging.
I wish therefore, Mr. Chairman, to congratulate C.B.C. authorities. They have performed fine work emphasizing especially the French fact in Canada.
Our compatriots who live in different environments welcome the possibility of getting in closer touch with the province of Quebec through the medium of the C.B.C.
As for us, we are glad to be able, through the C.B.C. to spread the splendid French culture. Not only is it of benefit to Frenchspeaking people in other provinces but it affords the English speaking population of Canada a means of adding to its own culture.

Mr. Chairman, on this occasion I think it is most appropriate for me, for perhaps the first time in my political
Supply-C.B.C.
career, to agree with the words of wisdom spoken this morning by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. His recommendations to the board of directors and the management of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation I think will be appreciated and acted upon.
Mr. Chairman, while I am on my feet I have a few remarks to make in a general way. Many speakers have urged an expansion of C.B.C. facilities into the outlying areas. I urge the management and the directors to give serious consideration to that request. In my opinion there is a strong duty on the part of the crown, whether it be an agency corporation or otherwise, to do what it can to develop our country.
Perhaps in doing so some consideration ought to be given to the sale of some of the existing facilities of the C.B.C. By that I mean studios and stations in the urban areas which should be self-supporting. It is impossible to ascertain whether some of the large C.B.C. set-ups are operating at a profit or a loss. If it should turn out that they are operating at a loss I am sure that free enterprise would be glad to take them over, and if that were done many items in the estimates could be reduced.
I hope when the minister replies he will make a statement concerning the progress in construction of the second microwave network into the maritimes. Last year the C.B.C. opened a new French language television station at Moncton which has been very much appreciated by the people of the maritimes who are within its range. However, it is not a live station, except for two hours a day when it has the facilities of the English language microwave. I hope the minister will cover this point when he replies so that the hundreds of thousands of Acadians in eastern Canada who are awaiting anxiously live television will some time in 1960 or 1961 have live French language television even though it may be originating in Montreal.
My final point concerns the way in which the estimates which appear on page 11 and again on page 128 are detailed. Under votes 43 and 44 for the international shortwave broadcasting service we get full details, even showing the amounts spent on fuel, postage, advertising, printing of publications and rent. A great part of that vote is spent in two communities, principally in the city of Montreal and in the town of Sackville, New Brunswick.
I think hon. members will be interested in knowing that as of April 1, 1960, there were a total of 27 transmitter stations at Sackville, New Brunswick, owned by the C.B.C. international shortwave service. Each

Supply-C.B.C.
of these stations has a call sign and is on the air pretty much right around the clock. They are strong stations; all of them are in the 50,000 watt range. On page 128 of the blue book we get the full details of expenditures of $2.3 million. This like the other items appears as a grant, but the big vote of nearly $70 million has the same phraseology on page 11 as it has on page 128. That amount of $70 million odd perhaps represents an amount well in excess of $100 million when we credit the revenue which the C.B.C. obviously gets.
Therefore I urge the minister and the board of directors to give more detail when preparing the estimates for the next fiscal year. The people of Canada and members of parliament in particular are entitled to that information.

Mr. Chairman, I am going to be quite brief, but I must say first of all that while I enjoy good music, opera, drama and all that sort of thing, I do not consider myself a beatnik. I represent the people of my constituency, who are a cultured people.
However, I rise to say that I was particularly interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre when he suggested to the minister that it would be a good idea to have a new production building in Vancouver and centralize the activities of the C.B.C. That may be very desirable, but no doubt an expenditure of that sort would run into millions of dollars. I rise once again to urge the minister and the C.B.C. and its senior officials to listen to the pleas of the hon. members for Kootenay East and Kootenay West, and make certain they provide the people in the out of the way places with radio and television, which facilities have been denied them to date, before they spend millions on a new building in Vancouver. When I say that, once again I repeat that I am speaking for the cultured people of the Kootenays.

Mr. Chairman, just one small matter. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate got up and made a rather unctuous statement about the law. He seems to be in the old tradition of law as a brooding omnipresence in the skies. I want to say that we hold no brief for the C.B.C. taking this particular program and putting it on the air in the circumstances which developed in connection with it, but to accept the hon. member's position so far as the law is concerned seems to me to overlook just what the law involves and the fact that laws shift and change.
Mr. Chairman, I discovered just the other day that I had committed, I will not give

the number but quite a host of parking violations, and I am sure there is not one human being in Canada but who is constantly breaking the law. We always have to bring the law into some kind of accordance with the public's point of view, and I think the point of view on this particular program on divorce which was mentioned by the hon. member for Timiskaming was really to the effect that the C.B.C. made a contribution to that discussion.
I say that because at the present time we have both shifting and conflicting views and attitudes toward divorce. Sooner or later we get a public consensus which leads in the end to a certain amount of hypocrisy with regard to the law, and I think the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is well aware that in many laws there is this hypocrisy.
In this particular case it seems to me that the C.B.C., whatever their judgment in the matter, were trying to make a contribution of that kind. Since I have asked the C.B.C. to be bold in its program rather than timid, I certainly do not feel that I want to turn around or that the members of our group want to turn around and clobber them over the head because of something which may have been a little too bold; but I certainly hope they will learn from this experience.

I would like to ask the
hon. gentleman a question, if he will permit it. Does the hon. member think that the public view of perjury is changing very much with changing customs?
I would certainly think the public view of perjury is changing with custom, and I think the public view on divorce is changing with custom.
That is a different matter, but I must say I am glad to be old-fashioned.

Mr. Chairman, I think it is just shocking to hear members of the C.C.F. party rise to defend this practice of the C.B.C. of having criminals appear on a program; boasting about their crimes, or lying, whatever the case may be; paying them for doing so, and then go on and suggest to this committee that they should be defended by the C.B.C. I think it is absolutely ridiculous that we should hear such suggestions coming from a political party of this country.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I want to make it clear that no action has been definitely criminal. There have certainly been no charges laid in this particular case. What we are suggesting is that this type of hypocrisy which is being displayed by the attorney general of Ontario is not to be desired, either. If it had been

stated that this was a program putting forward a composite view rather than an actual one, there probably would have been no objection to the program at all.
As far as I am concerned, I think many people would be willing to make a contribution to reimburse the C.B.C. in respect of this cost of $100, if it is the $100 that is worrying some hon. members. I am sure that such an amount could easily be raised by public subscription to pay for this particular program. The point I should like to make is this. Newspapers, in the past, have been successful in bringing injustices to the attention of the general public. No law is stagnant. The law should be changed as the need arises. I am sure this program intended to put forward one side of the argument. There are other sides, and the corporation would certainly be condemned if they did not put forward these views, too.
I do not think this is a matter of protecting a criminal, or anything of that nature. I doubt very much whether this young lady will ever be charged with anything, and I think that is the consensus in Ontario. It was merely a question of many members of the legal profession having to justify the position they appear to have taken, in the only manner they could, by discrediting the young lady in question-

speechtext: Order. The question of the conduct of solicitors has nothing to do with item 41 which is under consideration.

Mr. Chairman, this has been a long and interesting debate covering the whole gamut of human emotion and reactions to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, ranging from accusations of payola at Montreal to perjury in the C.B.C. If I attempted to deal with all the questions which have been raised I presume I would be keeping the committee here until six o'clock, and certainly, Mr. Chairman, you would have to rule me out of order on occasions, because many of the matters which have been raised have been out of order. However, it is often better to allow hon. members to say what they have in mind rather than raise points of order and become involved in an altercation as to how the rule applies, thereby wasting more time than has probably been spent as a result of the lax and reasonable attitude the Chair has taken during this debate.
Would the minister permit a question? Would he engage in some missionary activity on the treasury benches?

There have been many questions raised, and I do not intend to try to deal with them all in detail. I am sure hon.
Supply-C.B.C.
members do not expect me to do so, because there are many other matters which are engaging the attention of this committee. There is, of course, a close association between the board of broadcast governors and the C.B.C. Both the hon. member for Port Arthur and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate raised questions which are, perhaps, shall I say, hybrid; questions which impinge on the functions of both the board of broadcast governors and the C.B.C. I propose to reserve any comment on these matters until the item dealing with the board of broadcast governors is before us. Perhaps other issues will arise at the same time, and I think it will be economical of time if all such matters are dealt with on the latter item.
I think it is perhaps advisable, at the outset, to make a statement which one might expect not to have to make in this house. However, I want to make it clear not only to those who have taken part in this debate, and in particular to those who have been criticizing the C.B.C., but also to others in this house who perhaps have not taken part in this debate at all but who from time to time approach me asking why I permitted this or that to happen, or why I did or did not take action of a particular kind, that the minister is here only to report to parliament for the C.B.C. and that he has no power whatsoever to exercise control over that corporation. That is a matter of law, that is a matter of statute, and that is a matter of public policy.
Why?

All I can say is that this is the policy which has been followed in this parliament ever since the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and its predecessor were incorporated. I would point out as well, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate mentioned yesterday-this is one of the few matters with respect to which the hon. gentleman is prepared to give credit to R. B. Bennett-that it was a Conservative government under Mr. Bennett which created and incorporated the predecessor of the C.B.C., and the fundamental principle laid down at that time has been carried out throughout the years. That principle has been continued, and that has been the finding of every royal commission since which has made recommendations on the subject, in addition to about every parliamentary committee, and there have been around 20 of them since the corporation was established.
It is embarrassing at times. There are times when I should like to be able to exercise some control and power, but if there is sometimes embarrassment and frustration on the

Supply-C.B.C.
one side there is, on the other side, the obvious danger of having a public service such as the C.B.C. brought under political control. I am sure that on reflection one does not want to see political control exercised directly over the corporation, and that is the reason the situation is at it is.
I should also, perhaps, reiterate this. One hon. member did somewhat facetiously suggest that the proper thing for the government to do would be to sell the C.B.C. It is true that from time to time there have been suggestions that there are members of the party to which I have the honour to belong who are hostile to the C.B.C. and who would like to have it sold. Such suggestions have sometimes been specifically associated with this party. Undoubtedly that is true; there are a few of them. There are a few also, I think, in other parties from time to time. The Conservative party has no monopoly of that viewpoint by a long shot. There are people who have been hauled screaming and protesting into the twentieth century and still think they live in the eighteenth.
We respect their views, but certainly as far as this government is concerned I want to say again what has been said from time to time, namely that we believe in the C.B.C.; we support the corporation, and as long as this government is in power-and, I hope, as long as any government is in power-that policy will be maintained; because I am quite certain that if any government attempted to destroy that principle they would be heaved out of office so rapidly that they would never know what struck them.
It is true that from time to time as individuals we may disapprove of matters of programming, actions taken by the corporation, or actions by the board of boadcast governors. That is a privilege we all have, and I am far from saying for one moment that the corporation is anything like perfect. It has made its share of mistakes, and I am glad to see that some of them have been drawn to the attention of the committee during the present session. I hope these matters which have been brought forward will be investigated and dealt with-in fact I know they will be-and perhaps as a result the climate may be better than it has been heretofore.
But in so far as the general principle is concerned, I can say that this government believes in the C.B.C. as, I think, does every member who has spoken in this debate, including those who have been critical. They too have expressed appreciation of the contribution which the corporation is making to national unity. That is my view, though as I say there are many times when I could be critical. That general situation prevails,

and I want to make that clear at the outset in case any question is raised again at some time about the attitude of his government toward the C.B.C.
There were some specific questions raised by hon. members concerning their own constituencies. I know from experience that these matters are of great concern to individual hon. members. I feel that perhaps I should deal briefly with some of the detailed questions asked with respect to our television and radio services.

Before the minister proceeds, may I put a question and ask the minister when he is going to give television coverage to the constituency of Digby-An-napolis-Kings. I know it would be an embarrassing thing for him to ask himself.

Well, Mr. Chairman, the constituency of Digby-Annapolis-Kings does receive television coverage from private stations which are affiliated with the C.B.C. in Saint John. Part of my constituency receives television coverage from the C.B.C. station in Halifax. That depends on contours. In the little town in which I live the people who live on the hill receive excellent service from C.B.C. Halifax, but those living down where I live at the foot of the hill do not receive it at all. If I were a private member sitting in this house and someone else were standing in my place, I would be urging that improved coverage be given to the banner constituency of Digby-Annapolis-Kings so it would have the coverage it deserves. Modesty, of course, and my sense of responsibility toward all hon. members dictate that I have to look after their needs before pressing on the corporation the demands of my own constituency.
The hon. member for Churchill, who I see sitting here, who I see everywhere I turn when C.B.C. matters are raised, and who I see sometimes when I do not turn.-the hon. member sometimes is sitting in front of me-has raised again the question of coverage in northern Manitoba as did, of course, the hon. member for Dauphin and also the hon. member for Mackenzie, who referred to the other side of the provincial border-
And the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.

Yes, and the hon. member from the far reaches of Bonavista-Twillingate has also raised his voice in a plaintive cry that this area should be serviced. I am sure we all appreciate this evidence of co-operation. I am sure the hon. members for Churchill, Dauphin and Mackenzie recognize that this area has a unanimous claim for support

for better service from hon. members from all areas and all parties, and that this claim takes priority. Certainly if something is not soon done about it my life will be made absolutely impossible, because I will not be able to avoid the hon. member for Churchill even when I am eating lunch, which is about the only time the hon. gentleman is not asking me about this.
The president of the corporation when in Edmonton recently, on an occasion which has been criticized and to which we will perhaps refer later on, I hope, made certain specific statements with regard to the extension of coverage there. He said these matters will be included in the estimates for the coming year. I can assure the committee and the hon. members concerned that if this is included in the estimates, those particular items will be passed even if nothing else is passed, and thus there will be a commencement on the necessary television service in that area. It cannot all be developed at the one time; nevertheless there will be substantial amounts included in next year's estimates to start the development which I hope in the end will assure adequate service in that area, although some further engineering studies are necessary with respect to part of it.
The hon. member for Humber-St. George's raised the problem of radio coverage of station CBY. This is a very complicated problem and not an easy one to solve. The corporation is well aware of the problem there, but it bears on frequency allocations of other stations on the mainland and on planned changes the corporation has in mind for its own Halifax station. It relates to frequency allocations not only on the island but on the mainland and perhaps even as far as central Canada. This is a problem which is engaging the attention of the engineers of the corporation, and I am assured that in so far as engineers can be definite about any of these complicated problems, within a year to 18 months an adequate solution will have been found to the coverage problem.
The hon. member also raised the problem of television coverage, as did the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. The corporation advises me that over the next two or three years it expects to have progress to report in the general coverage problem in Newfoundland. The areas of Bonne Bay, Port aux Basques, Deer Lake and Steady Brook will probably come within the area of these plans. The solution suggested, of raising the power of the Harmon Field station, would not give the results that are needed.
Supply-C.B.C.
The hon. member for Halifax noted the requirements of the eastern section of Halifax county. I realize that there is in that area of my own province a need for adequate service. We are hopeful that the recent recommendation of the board of broadcast governors for approval of the Atlantic Broadcasting Limited application for a television station at Antigonish will solve this problem. It has not yet been dealt with by order in council. If the order in council is granted and that station goes into operation some time within the next year, we believe this area of the eastern Atlantic provinces will be much better served than ever before.
The situation around the west coast of Vancouver island and the Port Albemi section which was raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni will await developments resulting from the change in power and location of the Victoria television station. It is expected that the results of these changes will materially improve the reception on Vancouver island in those areas.
The hon. member for Kootenay West in his remarks mentioned the need of improved radio coverage in the Kootenay West and upper Arrow lakes districts, and I am glad to inform him that the corporation's plans for these areas are within a year to a year and a half of achievement if all goes well. Regarding the results of the Trail and Nelson low power television stations, we will have to await their operation, which is expected to start somewhere around next Christmas, before the corporation can assess the effectiveness of their coverage. The area of the Windermere valley also came in for mention by the hon. member for Kootenay East. This area is also slated within the foreseeable future for coverage by low power radio relay stations.
The situation in regard to the Mont Trem-blant-Mont Laurier area was also raised, and I am informed that the corporation is actively studying this area, making engineering surveys and endeavouring to clear a proper site to give television satellite coverage.
Mr. Chairman, before the minister proceeds, perhaps I could suggest a solution. Perhaps the Bomarc site could be used.

Mr. Chairman, I think that will be used for a much more important purpose. The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek questioned the provision of television in the Maple Creek area. Again, this is one of the areas under active investigation, and I am sure the hon. member is aware that this area receives radio service already.

Supply-C.B.C.
Some hon. members raised questions with respect to applications pending before the Department of Transport. I am informed that the following areas will be affected: St. Fintan's, Newfoundland, Senneterre, Quebec, Bancroft and Red Lake, Ontario.
There have been many other questions raised about individual areas. The hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort has raised with me on many occasions the question of service in the Tisdale area in Saskatchewan. I am advised by the C.B.C. that this is under study with the approval of the board for engineering surveys and cost and coverage estimates. All things going well and depending on any action by private stations, construction should be completed within the relatively near future, but certainly not before a year or perhaps a little more has elapsed.
I believe I have dealt with most of the geographical questions raised, but the hon. member for Westmorland a few moments ago raised a question about the connection of the microwave system with the French language station in Moncton. As the hon. member said, the French station there has the use of the English network for two hours a day when that network is not used for regular programming. I am told it will be approximately 18 months-give or take a few months but probably 18 months-before the French station is completely and permanently served by the microwave.
Some general questions were raised about the development of the corporation.

Mr. Chairman, before the minister leaves the question of future plans for so-called neglected areas, perhaps he would say something about what is in store in the near future for such localities in my riding as Dryden, Sioux Lookout and Ati-kokan? I am sure the officials will be quite familiar with the matter, because when I last met the president of the C.B.C. he told me I was perhaps his principal correspondent this session in the matter of mail with respect to the needs of this section.

Correspondent or corespondent? Apparently the C.B.C. has both. I will get the information from my officials for my hon. friend and give it to him, I hope, within a few minutes.
On the general construction program perhaps I should say this, taking radio first. It should be noted that the C.B.C. has in operation at the present time 73 of these low power relay stations. We all, of course, know the major ones. It has five applications pending before the Department of Transport, and is preparing eight other applications for submission to the department. Hon. members, of course, realize that these applications have

to be approved technically by the Department of Transport and then, having received technical approval, they usually-I think in every case-have to go before the board of broadcast governors for final approval. The corporation is conducting detailed engineering investigations in 19 other areas. It will be seen that this represents a total of 106 areas throughout the country. Of the stations in operation on the radio networks, 10 are French language relay stations and 63 are English language relay stations.
Let me turn now to television. The present situation is that of the 12 areas which have been licensed, seven are now in operation and five are under construction. The C.B.C. is preparing applications for nine other areas and is conducting detailed engineering investigations in 14 other locations, for a total of 35 areas. Of the 12 stations in operation or under construction eight will carry the English language service and four will carry the French language service.
The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm asked this question:
I should like to know, if possible, how many stations or networks, either French or bilingual, have been set up by the C.B.C. since 1958, in each province other than Quebec.
I am advised by the C.B.C. that the French language operations of the corporation are extensive. The C.B.C. operates a French language radio network from Edmonton, Alberta to southeastern Nova Scotia, servicing not only its own stations but also 22 privately owned affiliates. Since the beginning of 1958 the C.B.C. has installed and is operating low power radio relay French language transmitters in eight centres outside the province of Quebec, and a ninth is about to be installed.
In television, the C.B.C. operates a French network which links by recordings recently built C.B.C. television stations in Winnipeg and Moncton with its microwave network linking stations in Quebec and Ontario. It also provides French language television service to bilingual stations in Timmins and Sudbury, and has C.B.C. stations under construction in Sudbury and Sturgeon Falls in northern Ontario. The proposed C.B.C. station in Edmonton will also carry some French programs.
Another recent development of interest has been the establishment of a bilingual F.M. network, linking the corporation's F.M. stations in Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto, making available French language broadcasts in Toronto for the first time.
Generally, Mr. Chairman, that covers the development of the C.B.C. during the last year and the plans for extension in the immediate future.

The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River asked me a question a moment ago and I am advised by the officials of the C.B.C. that the Dryden and Sioux Lookout application is in preparation at the present time; Atikokan is some time away, but I cannot spell out the "some time". It is in the planning stage, at least. It is much more expensive than the first one I mentioned, namely Dryden and Sioux Lookout. The whole thing is in the course of planning, and at least part of it will be done in the relatively near future.
I think I have more or less covered the specific questions which were raised. One could deal at length with the criticism which has been levelled at the corporation. Perhaps hon. members will permit me to summarize that. In the first place we have been told that the corporation has refused to give information, and there has been much criticism of the statement in the estimates as being too concise and not giving enough information.
That criticism may have some justification. I think it has. But on the other hand I would point out to hon. members that the budget of the C.B.C. was tabled by me in the house some months ago and has been available to all hon. members. It is a break-down of the expenditures as set out in the estimates. In doing this we have simply carried out the practice that has been followed throughout the years. Maybe more detailed information should be given and there is no reason that I can see why, except for space, the information we put in the budget should not also be put in the estimates. The only reason it is not done is that it is already in the budget. The departmental estimates do not have to be tabled in the house. In the case of the C.B.C. therefore you have to look at both these documents in order to get a breakdown of the detail, the lack of which has been the subject of quite a bit of complaint here this year.
References have been made to the C.B.C. refusing to give information to the committee last year. I was a member of the committee but I attended only on two occasions. One was a very happy occasion and the other a very unfortunate one. As a matter of fact I suggested that the committee should not be given as much information as the officials were giving, and the committee turned around and by a substantial majority said that I did not know what I was talking about. The actual information was given, and I am told that whatever information was requested by the committee was placed in the hands of the committee.
It is not for me to come to the defence of that committee, but I do suggest that the
Supply-C.B.C.
problem lay with the administration of the committee and with the decisions it made as a committee of this house rather than with the corporation itself. In the past the position has been taken, which has been respected by this house and by the committees, rightly or wrongly, that information with respect to the amounts of moneys received by individuals has not been disclosed. That principle has been followed and I understand was followed by the committee last year.
There have been complaints also about waste and extravagance and, as I understand, even including what is called payola. A suggestion was made that payola took various forms, not only in so far as cash was concerned but also in other forms. I am not in a position to comment on that in any way, shape or form. In most instances the statements were of a very general nature.
The hon. member for St. Mary saw me after the debate the other day and gave to me a list of names, suggesting that if those matters were investigated at least some of the accusations made here could be substantiated. I told him that I did not want to take the list at that time because I would probably lose it, but I do not think it is a matter of my taking such lists anyway, though I went on to say in that connection that if any person had any information of that nature and would pass it on to me I would certainly see that it was turned over to the officials of the C.B.C.
That may not be satisfactory, because I think we can realize quite frankly that there are some suspicions on the part of some hon. members with respect to some of the officials of the C.B.C., particularly Radio Canada. Whether that situation is justified or not is not for me to say but I want to make this very plain. We have a board of directors, and part of the responsibility of that board is to deal with financial problems, with waste and extravagance and anything of that nature. I could go into that at length, but I do not propose to do so at this hour unless I am asked to develop it.
The chairman of that board of directors is Mr. Robert Dunsmore of Montreal, one of the outstanding businessmen in Canada. I can assure any hon. member that if he does not want to deal with the C.B.C., if he will talk to Mr. Dunsmore, or Mr. Dunsmore will talk to any member here when he is in Ottawa, and if the member will give him the information, it will be studied in detail, so that we shall have a complete investigation of any matter whatsoever that any hon. member feels should be brought in and studied by the directors. That is one of their responsibilities; that is why Mr. Dunsmore

Supply-C.B.C.
was asked to take the chairmanship of the finance committee. We felt that as an experienced businessman he could deal with this matter, and he certainly will. I would ask any hon. member to bring to his attention any of these matters which have been referred to here today or at any other time.
Now, as has been said, there has been a substantial amount of criticism here about the Radio Canada end of the Canadian broadcasting coverage. This particular part of the corporation has come in for very substantial praise as well, and has received very little criticism on the basis of its operations. I am prepared to admit, however, that no organization is perfect. If there are matters which should be drawn to our attention, if there are matters connected with partisanship or with extravagance or graft, then I am assured by the officers of the corporation sitting in front of me that they are going to investigate every matter which has been brought to their attention. I can assure you also that, regardless of that, the board of directors and the chairman of the finance committee will make a very careful study of anything that might be brought to their attention. I do not believe it is necessary for me to go further into that phase of the subject at this time.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate raised two specific problems in connection with the C.B.C. I might say, Mr. Chairman, that I have not looked up last year's debate but I think you could find those problems almost verbatim in the debate which took place a year ago.
My memory is not that good.

I think no greater tribute could be paid to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation than the fact that an able, astute critic such as the hon. member could only bring up matters with which he dealt extensively last year. I replied to those last year, and I do not believe any good purpose could be served by spending much time on them now. He again criticized the board of directors in appointing a chairman other than the president, and suggested that was illegal.

Well, we did ask questions. For my part, I am still waiting for answers to several of mine. Only recently I asked a question, and have not yet received any answer either from the minister or from the C.B.C.
I know that at times it is not easy to find the information requested. I know it requires a little time to prepare a satisfactory answer both for the member and for everyone.
However, I should like to repeat that we are entitled to ask questions on the orders of the day. Let us, then, have answers without any beating about the bush.
I am sorry that it should be so but last year, a member dared ask, on the orders of the day, what income was being earned by some commentator or performer. The answer was that it was not C.B.C. policy to reply to that type of question.
The principle was laid down that salaries earned by C.B.C. staff must not be made known.
Yet, take a look at the public accounts and you will find there the salaries of officials earning $8,000 or more.
Salaries of members of the house are listed, and a fact of which the public seems to be unaware is that members too have taxes to pay, I take this opportunity to set the record straight and to emphasize that fact. We have to pay taxes on our indemnity. The public knows what indemnity is paid to members and what salaries are paid to ministers.
The public also knows what salaries are paid to the chairman and high officials of the C.B.C. Why should we be denied knowledge of what salary is being paid to certain C.B.C. commentators when we have every reason to believe that favouritism exists within the corporation and that certain performers and commentators are given preference over other persons who are at least as talented and competent, and when we know that such persons have no say in the matter.
In reply to the questions we asked, the minister set forth certain principles. He seemed to back up the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate who, with his winning

Mr. Chairman, I am prepared to believe that what is quite acceptable to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is not nearly so to others who are truly democratic and who believe that a sense of responsibility is still to be found within a democratic government.
Who is answerable to the public for the C.B.C.? Who, in the C.B.C., has to render accounts and is subject to sanctions if the public is not satisfied? Surely not the minister, who has no power whatsoever; surely not the government since it has nothing to say and is taken to task as soon as a minister or a member wants to shed light on the goings on in the C.B.C.?
What has happened to the principle of responsibility of the people's representatives?
Are we going to keep voting amounts of $70 million to an agency which refuses to report on the use it is making of those funds? Is it an encroachment upon the freedom and autonomy of the C.B.C. to ask that its directors account for the public funds entrusted to it?
If we look up the estimates of the C.B.C. for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1961, we find on page 11 of the estimates that we are asked to vote $71,739,400. We see, too, that there are more details in the summary on page 11 than under "Details of services", on page 128 of the blue book.
And when we ask questions, we cannot get answers. It seems that the government does not want to be in a position to answer. that we, government members, have no right to ask questions. Yet when we ask questions about some other department, we are entitled to answers. Where is government responsibility in a case like that? It may be that C.B.C. are giving adequate answers but it seems to me-and I am sorry to say so -that there is wide discrepancy between what we are told by C.B.C. officials in answer to our specific questions and what people repeat derisively about the C.B.C. and the federal government whenever they talk of the corporation.
Mr. Chairman, even though I touched upon this matter last week, I repeat that there are people who would like to do away with the C.B.C., and have its network put up for sale. I do not agree with this view, and I am saying so right away. But, it must be recognized that serious-minded citizens have suggested such a step and, if I remember rightly, certain associations even made this suggestion to the Fowler commission. I remember that in 1955 or 1956 the Federation of the Junior Chambers of Commerce of the province of Quebec made the suggestion that the federal government should give up C.B.C. operations and sell its network to private interests.
Let me say at once that I do not agree with that suggestion. But, if deficits continue to pile up, and to soar drastically, without stricter and more efficient supervision, there wifi probably be more people who will ask that the C.B.C. be sold off to private enterprise, which, to my mind, would be calamitous. However, it must be admitted that those people are making a serious suggestion when they recommend that the C.B.C. give up operating its network, and looking after its organization, even though it might prescribe that private networks carry certain

cultural programs, that for a certain number of hours private stations must produce cultural programs, at no other compensation than the cost of time on the air, in order to contribute efficiently to the development and extension of Canadian culture.
That solution is worthy of serious consideration, even though I feel it would give rise to difficulties, perhaps as insuperable as those now being experienced.
Again, about the C.B.C., I wish to deal with the matter of purchases instead of sales.

Let the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) not rejoice too soon; we have no intention of destroying the French network. We are proud of it, we are proud of the C.B.C.'s achievements.
We know that the English network is not without sin either and members from other provinces deserve credit for their patience in concealing them. We, however, are candid enough to expose, in the place where they ought to be exposed, the wrongs of the French network.
We want to protect the C.B.C.'s reputation, and we want some light to be cast, once and for all, on the charges that are being made. If severe action is in order, let there be severe action. If congratulations are in order, let there be congratulations. However, let us bring the whole thing out into the open.
As I have said before, I was elected to this house in 1958. The C.B.C. came under fire in three sessions, and I refrained from making any remarks for fear of harming the corporation. I was reluctant to deal with this matter, because I was running the risk of being accused of malevolence towards C.B.C. networks.
I intervened during this session because I realized that, in the last three years, not only have the charges continued but they have grown stronger, as have also the facts adduced in support of those charges.
During the C.B.C. French network strike in 1959, the strike leaders, including Rene

The most violent of them, with Rene Levesque leading the way, scathingly denounced the C.B.C.'s president, Mr. Alphonse Ouimet, at a time when he was ill, knowing as they did that he could not defend himself. During the strike, certain C.B.C. officials were likewise denounced. Some, like Andre Ouimet, assumed their responsibilities. Whether their attitude was warranted or not, that is beside the point. They would have us say, during the strike, that everything was black at the C.B.C., and the next day they wanted us to turn around and say that everything was white, simply because of attempted blackmail by certain people who were making the most of the strike-including certain people I do not wish to name-
Go ahead, name them. Name them.

-because I do not want to harm their reputation-because after the strike, in the face of the management's weakness, a little clique was formed which allowed the strike leaders to get jobs as commentators or producers of the best programs. I believe the minister has been most able and that he is most worthy of congratulation on the forthright and blunt manner in which he has at all times defended those basic principles and purposes. As long as we are obliged to endure a Conservative government in Canada we should not like to see the C.B.C. moved to any other minister.

I believe efficiency could be enhanced a bit there.

I should also like to offer the personal proposal that the C.B.C. might make more use of less expensive film showings rather than engage in repeat programs. On Monday last there was a repeat program. On Sunday, when the listening audience must have been very large, C.B.C. television used two half-hour repeat programs that had been seen previously. I know that the lack of adequate resources is likely the explanation. However, I believe that other use might be made of that time and that it need not necessarily involve a great deal of expenditure.
I should also like to offer the proposition that in arranging for the engagement of commentators and interviewers, the work be spread around a little more. People do not like to see the same individual commentators and interviewers appear repeatedly to the exclusion of others and to the exclusion of a little more variety. We have over 100 members in the press gallery here. There are other press galleries in Canada. There are extremely able newspapermen and other commentators and observers from one end of Canada to the other. People rather resent being obliged to listen to the same commentators over and over again, especially when they know there are many more able people available in Canada than are being utilized by the C.B.C.
I have mentioned previously the original principles and purposes of the C.B.C. The hon. members who preceded me seems to lack an understanding of the relationship of the C.B.C. to the government. As I have always understood it, the C.B.C. is not an institution of government. The C.B.C. is an institution of this parliament and is responsible to this parliament rather than to the government of the day. It is only as a convenience and only for the sake of reporting that a minister of the government is the spokesman for the C.B.C. when it is obliged annually to appear before this House of Commons.
That situation in effect means that the people of Canada who own the C.B.C. have elected themselves a board of directors composed of 265 members of parliament. However, the members of parliament in their wisdom have decided to entrust matters of management to an appointed board of directors, and I believe that it ill behooves us to begin to interfere in small details of management with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.

If we are unhappy with the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, I believe that we should then be bold enough to say that in our opinion the board of directors is not fulfilling its obligations and ought to be replaced. We have noted with a little bit of dismay that the many attacks on the various phases of the operations of the C.B.C. as they have been recorded in this House of Commons within the last number of days have been represented by the radio and the newspapers as almost complete dissatisfaction on the part of the House of Commons with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. We feel that this is a misunderstanding. I myself have noted the many hon. members in this committee who have expressed approval. After commenting on some phase or other of the operation, either favourably or otherwise, most members of this committee have none the less expressed their over-all approval of this institution, namely the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Yet I believe our newspapers have tended to highlight the attacks on little details of operation, and have not adequately reported to the Canadian people that in the main the House of Commons has expressed its desire to have the C.B.C. continue to serve us as a national and publicly owned radio and television broadcasting network.
We endorse-and we should like to underline our opinion-the need for a national and publicly owned radio and television network because we believe that without it, and if we were obliged to depend on private enterprise, there might not even be a network at all of any kind in Canada because it might not be economically possible for private enterprise to establish such a network. Even if they were able to establish a national network we believe that many more communities than there are now would be obliged to do without either C.B.C. radio or television services. There would also be no hope of those communities which do not now have those services ever getting them unless they can get them from a publicly owned operation.
We also feel the need for a national and publicly owned network because we are concerned with the raising of the level of culture all across Canada. Perhaps I should not say "the raising of the level of culture" but rather the enjoyment of culture. I believe that

expression has less of a connotation to it. We do know that of necessity privately owned broadcasting facilities have to cater in the matter of taste to the lines of least resistance, and that if all radio and television in Canada was in the hands of private enterprise there would inevitably be a degradation of the levels of Canadian culture. I say this without any malice but because I believe the mere law of economics would enforce a condition of that kind to arise.
We have been a little surprised, though perhaps we ought not to be, at the terrific controversy which has arisen within the last several years all across Canada about this matter of the C.B.C. and the whole field of radio and television broadcasting. The C.B.C. was moving along rather smoothly for a number of years and seemed to know where it was going. On the whole there was very little dissatisfaction across Canada. I believe it is a good thing that after many years there has been this public look taken at what is happening in the field of broadcasting.
The attacks we have heard over the last few years I believe were inevitable, and I hope that all these proposals which have been made were made out of a sincere effort to be useful. I am not too sure that this is necessarily so after looking at some of the remarks which have been made.
After having been reorganized so that there is now a board of broadcast governors and a board of directors of the C.B.C.; after the house has appointed several committees which over the years have investigated all the ramifications, we feel that the time has about arrived for a decision to be made as to the validity today of the original principles and purposes. We feel there ought to be a consolidation of opinion and that the board of directors of the C.B.C.-I feel we owe this to them-should be given a clear indication of what their responsibility is and what the Canadian people really expect of them. They should also then be given the green light to go ahead with the least possible hindrance in implementing the resolution of the Canadian people in that regard.
I regret that in his reply the minister did not deem it advisable to enunciate very clearly what in his opinion the role of the C.B.C. is expected to be over the course of the next few years, so that this committee might have expressed its endorsation of such a general statement of broad, basic principles on the part of the minister, or of an amendment if it were deemed advisable to announce an amendment of these basic principles. speechtext: Has the minister statement to make on this item at this time?

Yes, Mr. Chairman. This is the vote dealing with the board of broadcast governors. I have a statement here, the whole of which I do not think it is necessary for me to read at this time. It deals with the statutory powers of the board, the background and so forth. I will read the latter part, however.
The decision by the government announced in July 1959 to permit the licensing of an additional television station in centres already served by a Canadian television station will add significantly to the work load of the board. As a result of this policy it has been necessary for the board to hold special public hearings to consider applications for a second television station in Edmonton, Calgary, Halifax and Ottawa in 1960-61.
