Similar hearings were held in Winnipeg, Vancouver, Montreal and Toronto in 1959-60. The board will also be expected to consider applications for other new stations, increases in power and changes in facilities that are referred to it regularly by the department. It is expected

that the board will hold a minimum of six public hearings, six meetings of the board, three meetings of the executive committee and a number of other meetings of the subcommittees of the board during 1960-61.
The present establishment of the board provides for 31 positions, including those of the chairman, vice-chairman and the full time member. At the present time 28 of these positions have been filled. The three full time members are appointed to their positions by the governor in council for a period of seven years, and the full tune staff of the board are all appointed under the provisions of the Civil Service Act. The 12 part time members are appointed by the governor in council for a period of five years.
Although the estimates before the house indicate an increase of $98,420 over the amount voted for the previous fiscal year, the actual increase will be closer to $75,000 as the actual expenditure of the board for the fiscal year 1959-60 will be approximately $223,000. Supplementary estimates in the amount of $23,138 have been submitted by the board for the fiscal year 1959-60. In this respect it should be pointed out that the estimate of $200,000 for 1959-60 was prepared by the board less than six months after it had been established and was, inevitably, based on projected operations of the board, the cost of which could not be fully foreseen and, in fact, it proved necessary to submit supplementary estimates to provide additional funds.
In the 1959-60 estimates the amounts provided for allowances and travelling expenses proved inadequate due mainly to the necessity for the board to hold public hearings of longer duration to consider the numerous applications for second television licences resulting in additional expenditure for per diem allowances for the part time members and travelling and living expenses. On the other hand, the actual expenditure against the amount provided for salaries in 1959-60 was more than was needed due to the fact that some of the positions approved were not filled as quickly as had been anticipated.
The board held its first public hearing in January, 1959 and has therefore been in actual operation for 18 months. During this period the regulatory and administrative functions of the board have inevitably increased and additional staff has been added to properly discharge the responsibilities of the board. Apart from the continuing necessity to hold public hearings, the board has within the past year issued radio station broadcasting regulations, radio (T.V.) regulations and a statement of policy on political and controversial broadcasting.

I think that is all that is indicated at the moment, Mr. Chairman. Of course, I shall be glad to attempt to deal with any questions raised by hon. members.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister will remember that the other evening when I thought this vote was under consideration I began to make certain observations in connection with it. I hope that in anything I have to say at this time neither the minister nor anyone associated with him will consider what I have to say as personal. After all, we on this side of the chamber have certain obligations and duties to perform and it seems to me that in performing these properly there has to be criticism.
At the outset of my remarks the other day I stated that I believed the policy in connection with these applications was that first applications were made to the Minister of Transport who after having determined through his officers whether there was any objection from a technical standpoint or a telecommunications standpoint would then pass them on to the board of broadcast governors who in turn would hold public hearings across Canada, hear the evidence, and they would then be returned to the Minister of Transport after which he would submit them to the governor in council for approval.
Following what the minister has said it would appear that the board of broadcast governors has held a number of public hearings in this country, with the following results: One was held in Halifax where a licence was recommended by the board in favour of CJCH Limited which now operates radio station CJCH Halifax and which would be expanded to include Canastel Broadcasting Corporation of Toronto, a wholly owned subsidiary of Association Television (ATV) of England; major individual shareholders are Gerald E. Martin, Halifax, chartered accountant, and Finlay MacDonald who manages CJCH.
Montreal-English language station-Canadian Marconi Company which already operates radio station CFCF, Montreal, and which is controlled by Canmar Investments Limited, wholly owned subsidiary of English Electric Company Limited of London.
Montreal-French language station-Paul L'Anglais and associates, headed by Montreal French film distributor Joseph A. DeSeve.
Ottawa-E. L. Bushnell Television Company, headed by the former C.B.C. vicepresident and including the Granada TV Network of England and NTA Telefilm (Canada) Limited which includes United States participation.
Supply-C.B.C.
Toronto-Baton Aldred Rogers Broadcasting Limited, controlled by the Toronto Telegram and including veteran broadcaster Foster Hewitt or radio station CKFH Toronto, T.V. personality Joel Aldred and Paul Nathanson of Sovereign Film Distributors Limited.
Winnipeg-Ralph S. Misener, Winnipeg businessman and sportsman, associated with Lloyd E. Moffat, owner of radio station CKY Winnipeg, Walter E. Kroeker, president of radio station CFAM Altona, Manitoba; Roland Couture of radio station CKSB St. Boniface, Manitoba; and T. O. Peteirson, director of a Winnipeg investment syndicate.
Edmonton-The publicly owned C.B.C.
Calgary-CFCN Television Limited, headed by Gordon Love, president of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, and members of his family who now operate radio station CFCN Calgary.
Vancouver-Van tel Broadcasting Company Limited, headed by 34-year-old Arthur Jones, now head of a Vancouver film production company and including several British Columbia businessmen.
Before dealing with some of these licences in the manner I wish to I should like to put a question to the minister. The hon. gentleman may respond to it later if he wishes. Of those licences I have mentioned, how many have been approved by the governor in council and how many still remain to be approved?
Following what has been said by my colleague the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate I wish now to say a word with respect to the steps necessary for the establishment of a station. What are the principles? What is the manner in which the board of broadcast governors goes about the granting of these licences? It would seem to me that the main requirement for a station is a frequency channel. Without that a licence cannot be granted. These frequency channels belong not to an individual group. They are part of the public domain, the property of the Canadian people, and they should be treated as such.
In 1953 when I occupied the position of minister of transport I outlined at some length the position of the government and I put on the record a statement which I should like to repeat again today. I believe this statement has a great bearing on the granting of these rights.
That statement with which I was in complete accord was made by a former prime minister of this country, the Right Hon. Mr. Bennett, when he discussed the principles dealing with matters of this sort on second reading of a bill which he introduced in the house on May 18, 1932 as reported at page 3035 of Hansard of that date. I shall quote

I want to say something about the subject to which my hon. friend from Laurier has just referred. I had something to say on this subject at the time the motion was before the house to set up the committee on broadcasting. I did say something about it on an earlier occasion outside the house. I think I should, if the minister will not take a technical objection, put on the record again what I said the other day as recorded at page 5195 of Hansard, because I want to deal with it. I would rather put it on exactly as I said it than to paraphrase it, which I would have a perfect right to do.
I was referring then to the granting of the private television licence in the city of Toronto and I said in part:
It is very hard now to understand this extraordinary decision which was made in Toronto in

Supply-C.B.C.
favour of a newspaper whose proprietor, according to all reports, months before the application was heard by the board went about saying that there was no need for them to hold any hearing because he already had it. It does seem to me that is something which needs very careful investigation, as well as the whole policy underlying that situation.
Subsequently, the publisher of the Toronto Telegram, Mr. John Bassett, apparently took notice of what I had said in the house. I am sorry I do not have an extract from his own newspaper, but I have one from the Toronto Star which I think would be most scrupulous to report him correctly, for obvious reasons.
If the shoe were on the other foot, what would then be the case?

I would think they would be very careful to report each other correctly because of the rule of law in this country, if not for any other reason. In any event, I think I should read what Mr. Bassett had to say. The news item reads this way:
John Bassett, publisher of the Telegram, denied today that he boasted about having a licence for Toronto's private T.V. station before the board of broadcast governors awarded it to a company controlled by him.
The charge was made in the commons yesterday by J. W. Pickersgill (L-Bonavista-Twillingate) during a debate on the board's choices for private T.V. ownership.
Then it goes on to say something about the hon. member for Port Arthur and Mr. Bassett is quoted as having said:
"Mr. Pickersgill's statement is absolutely untrue," Mr. Bassett said. "I haven't spoken to Mr. Pickersgill about anything important for the last 10 years -other than just a few how-do-you-dos."
That is quite correct. Mr. Bassett and I are not what you would call bosom pals, and I have not spoken to him on many occasions, certainly not beyond ordinary politenesses. However, I thought Mr. Bassett's denial very odd because I never said he told me this. I said that there was a rumour, and that is all I said. Perhaps I was wrong in saying there was a rumour without having more than a rumour, but this rumour was not the casual kind of rumour. This rumour had been published by a very reputable journalist, Mr. Pierre Berton, in the Toronto Star on April 1. I think that this part of what Mr. Berton had to say ought to be on the record because I think it does justify a member of parliament using it as a basis and, to the best of my knowledge, no action was taken against Mr. Berton to get him to withdraw this statement. Here is the way it read:
Please, Mr. Bassett, don't put away that crystal ball.
I have been worrying about the Toronto Telegram which recently lost the services of one of its columnists, Dr. Spencer Thornton.

The article continues to some extent about that, which is not really relevant, and then goes on:
I suggest this because Mr. Bassett's prescience in the matter of the private T.V. license is now the talk of Toronto. He is being congratulated on all sides for what may well be the greatest piece of crystal-gazing since the late Mackenzie King put away his glass ball.
X don't really know whether Mr. Bassett was peering into the future via the Telegram horoscope, or if he simply switched to Wildroot cream oil, the hair tonic that gives you confidence, but he has certainly been exuding assurance for several months regarding Channel Nine.
This is in Mr. Berton's style which is not exactly my style. It goes on at some length but the most significant paragraph of it is this:
So certain was he of victory that his architects went ahead and produced complete detailed drawings for his million-dollar T.V. building-a job that takes several weeks. The blueprints were rolling off within four days of the B.B.G.'s announcement that John Bassett was the fortunate winner.
Other evidence is also given that he felt that he had this licence. But whether he had or not is not the main point. I merely put this on the record because it is common gossip; and I would have thought that if Mr. Bassett felt this statement that he had forecast this decision was untrue he would have taken steps to correct it when it appeared in the Toronto Star. But again, as I say, that is not the main point. The main point is the point which I made in Toronto and which I made again in the House of Commons, namely the point that as a matter of public policy-and up until very recently this has appeared to be the policy not merely of the previous administration but of the present administration-I believe it is undesirable for television licences, which are much more monopolistic in character than are radio licences, to be given to newspapers or the proprietors of newspapers or corporations in which newspapers have a substantial and controlling interest.
I think that procedure is undesirable when there is in the place another applicant who is equally qualified or approximately equally qualified to have that franchise or that bit of the public domain, as my hon. friend from Laurier pointed out. I say that we took the position when we were in office that if there was no other applicant or no other qualified applicant to provide a television station, then a place should not be deprived of it because the only applicant was a newspaper or a newspaper publisher or a company in which a newspaper or a newspaper publisher had a substantial interest. I think this would be a ridiculous position to take.
Mr. Bassett apparently thought that he had found a beautiful reply to me when I spoke

in Toronto last May because on May 4 he published an illuminated article. It was illuminated with an extremely attractive sketch which I take it is supposed to be me in oilskins and in the usual costume in which I am portrayed in that newspaper which has given me a great deal of favourable publicity for which I have always been grateful and for which I have never had to pay, but which I do not feel puts me under any sense of obligation which prevents me from criticizing the newspaper or its publisher if I feel so inclined in this free country. It is headed "Politician with a short memory... Pick Clouds the Airwaves". I must say I thought that was rather flattering. I had a feeling that perhaps the great public was not quite as much interested in what I had said as was Mr. Bassett himself or whoever wrote this for him. This article purports to be written from Ottawa and it is marked "Special". I suspect, of course, that it was a synthetic piece but it also purports to give a list of all the television stations and all the radio stations that are owned by newspapers, newspaper publishers or people having any connection with newspapers. Since Mr. Bassett, this favoured person of the B.B.G. and the present government who was given the best piece of the public domain available in Canada, thought it was quite important to put these arguments forward I think it is equally important to have the facts put forward about them.
Hear, hear. Let us get them.

Here they are. Here is a list of these television stations that are owned or partly owned by newspapers where the licence was granted in the time of the previous administration on the recommendation of the board of governors of the C.B.C. I have gone through as many as I could of the notices of application and of the recommendations and subject to error which I may have made because I was obliged to do this research myself and to do it rather hastily I think that my facts will be found to be correct.
There was a licence granted in Calgary. This was one of the very first applications and it was granted to the only applicant so that it comes completely within the terms of the statement I made at the beginning of May of this year in Toronto, whatever date it was. There was a licence granted in Lethbridge and that was not granted until nearly a year after the early application and it was granted to the only applicant. There was one in Regina granted, among the early ones, to the only applicant. There was one granted in London to the London Free Press,
Supply-C.B.C.
a newspaper which has over the years not been notoriously favourable, as everyone knows, to the Liberal party.
Oh, oh.

And that was granted to the only applicant. There was a licence granted to Niagara Television Limited in Hamilton in which a minority interest is held by the Southam Company. There is no control there. It was among the first and it was granted to the only applicant. Then there was one granted to the Saint John Publishing Company of Saint John, New Brunswick and it was granted to the only applicant. The only two cases I have been able to find in Mr. Bassett's list where there was any question at all of any other applicant entering into the picture were the station in Kingston and the station in Peterborough.
What about St. John's?

I am just dealing with Mr. Bassett's researches or Mr. Bassett's special report. I am not dealing with any other cases or any other hon. member. I happen to know about one or two others myself, as a matter of fact, which I will deal with if any questions are raised. But in the case of these two stations, one at Kingston and one at Peterborough, they were both originally applied for by the same company and they were both deferred. Then subsequently, when no other applicant at all turned up for the Kingston station, the licence was granted to another company which was divorced from the original company to some degree. I think it is a well known fact that two very prominent publishers, one of whom is connected with the Liberal party and one of whom was a Conservative candidate in a not too distant election in one of the constituencies in the suburbs of Toronto and who now own a very substantial part of all communications in this country and two or three other countries, were joint owners.
I do not think it could be argued that it was because of any particular preference the previous administration would have had for that particular kind of set-up that that was done. In fact, in the case of the Peterborough station according to the records another applicant ultimately turned up after the application was deferred three or four times and the other applicant had apparently no local backing according to what the C.B.C. recommended, I presume quite honestly, and the application was not recommended. Finally the application of the Kawartha Broadcasting Company was.
I might say that one or two others were held up. In the case of Saskatoon the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix was the first applicant

Supply-C.B.C.
and their application was held up until another applicant turned up and then the Star-Phoenix application was denied, and I could give other cases of that kind too.
When these television licences were being recommended by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation they were complete monopolies. That is to say, you could not have one television station nearer than 40 miles from another and certain steps were taken to see they did not invade each other's territory. That was in the experimental stages when a lot of people did not think that in many places television could be made to pay at all. That is why in many cases no other applicant, except a publisher or a newspaper or someone connected therewith, ever turned up because I assume no one else felt the risk was worth it.
The fact that ever since the beginning of radio broadcasting in this country radio stations have been owned by newspapers and radio stations have been all through our history competitive seems to me to have nothing to do with the argument at all, and as far as I am concerned I never at any time said it had. But what I do think is fundamental is that we do not want monopoly of sources of information. The government is pretending to try to strengthen the combines legislation in this country, although we do not think it is. We do not think it is desirable, wherever it can be practically avoided, to have this common ownership of multiple sources of communication.
The Toronto situation was a particularly glaring one. My opinion was, as I expressed it in Toronto, that the B.B.G. should have thrown out the applications of all three newspapers at the opening of their hearing, because in the judgment they gave afterwards they said they had a hard time making up their minds because all the applications were so good. They had thrown out every other application from a newspaper up to that time, in Winnipeg and Vancouver, but suddenly here in Toronto, where if my memory serves me there were six other applicants, they apparently transgressed what I thought had always been understood by hon. members opposite as well as our party to be undesirable in principle, namely to have newspapers own these facilities when anyone else of competence was available to own them. Why that should have been departed from in that case is hard to see.
Will the hon. gentleman permit a question?
Certainly.

Would he not agree that a few years ago the government of which the hon. member was a minister granted a [Mr. Pickersgill.J
television licence to a newspaper owner in St. John's, and would he not agree that that television company has been doing a very good job? At the time I believe the C.B.C. also applied for that franchise.

The hon. member is not quite accurate in his facts. In those days the C.B.C. did not apply for licences at all. The C.B.C. was the licensing authority, but I do not want to seem to quibble.
It is true that the C.B.C. was willing to build a station there if the government would put up the money. It is true that there was a private applicant and that the government in its wisdom decided that there should not be a C.B.C. station at St. John's, as it also decided there should not be one at Saint John, or Fredericton, or Charlottetown, or Calgary, or Edmonton, or Regina, or Saskatoon. The decision which was made by the previous administration, which was made by the government as I suggested earlier in the debate on the C.B.C. estimates should be done, was as to the places in which public money should be used to establish these capital facilities. Whether we were right or wrong we decided that if we established public stations in Vancouver, in Winnipeg, in Toronto, in Ottawa, in Montreal and in Halifax, we would have enough stations to provide national network coverage and that the rest of the field should be left to private initiative.
What about Corner Brook?
The Corner Brook decision was made by the hon. member's friends, not by the previous administration.
That was no friend of ours.
That is not really relevant, but the Corner Brook station was not decided upon until after the present government came into office.
But by the old board.

I am talking about what the previous government did, and if the hon. member thinks I should be replied to perhaps he will reply afterwards because I should like to carry on the thread of my argument.
The position we took was that in order to get national coverage in Canada and in order to minimize the cost to the taxpayers of the country we should establish enough stations to create a network, that everywhere else we should give in each area a monopoly for the time being to see whether television was practicable, and up until the time we left office that remained the situation.
The Fowler commission was asked to report on this matter and they made a report which

we did not have time or opportunity to act upon but which has, after three years, now been acted upon by the present government. That action was the policy of establishing second and competitive stations in the places where the C.B.C. had stations and in one or two other places, like Edmonton and Calgary, where it did not.
I say that what we find impossible to understand is why there should have been this departure from this time-honoured principle. I think it is regrettable that the government, which has the final responsibility, did not reject the recommendation of the B.B.G. in this case. It should have rejected it, not on the ground that these people were not as competent to do the work as somebody else-I have no opinion on that at all and I would not venture an opinion because I do not think it is desirable that we should try to adjudicate things like that here in parliament-but the board having said they had such difficulty in choosing between the applicants and it being objectionable in principle, it seems to me the government should have said "We do not want a licence given to a newspaper or to a station controlled by a newspaper if there is another equally good applicant, so take this thing back and hear it over again". That it seems to me would have been the right course.
We now have in this Ottawa decision an even more frightening thing, because here we have a licensee picked out from among five, I think there were, the one licensee who seems to be partly owned and controlled by television organizations in another country. The whole purpose surely of the development of broadcasting in this country and of the development of private broadcasting is to give an expression to local and national conditions, local and national aspirations and to local and national talent. The idea that we are going to have a station largely owned by one of the leading television companies in the United Kingdom is-
Which one?

Granada. It does seem to me to raise very grave questions indeed. The whole purpose of public broadcasting in the first place is to keep it Canadian. We have never interpreted that in any narrow manner or sense. The C.B.C. from the beginning has taken the best of the things from the United States and the best of the things from the United Kingdom, but it begins to look, from what we hear, and here again we need some reassurance from the government, as though this Ottawa station is to become the focus of a network which is to bring in television from the outside.
Supply-C.B.C.
Apart altogether from that I express, as I have expressed in the past with regard to the Canadian Pacific Air Lines, and, of course, the railways, concern with this situation because as we know there was very grave concern about the whole question of so-called competition in this field, and I say "so-called competition" because it is not really competition, as everybody knows. In Toronto at the present time you are going to have a public station and one private station and there is no room for anyone else because there is no channel. If this is going to mean in Vancouver, Toronto or Halifax-and I think that from an economic standpoint the situation in Halifax can only be marginal-the private corporation is going to bring in film or other material more or less dumped from the United States and the United Kingdom in order to pick up advertising revenue by filling up the air waves with material of this sort, while leaving the C.B.C. to carry the other material and the taxpayers to pick up the tab, then I do not like that at all. That is the direction in which it appears we are moving now. That is why we feel we should move very prudently with regard to this matter. My hon. friend from Laurier has pointed out the way in which the Canadian Pacific transcontinental air service is affecting the balance sheet of the T.C.A., and I am worried about how these things are going to develop with respect to the balance sheet of the C.B.C.
No doubt this will be slightly out of order, but hon. members do read, and they undoubtedly read the editorial about C.B.C. finances which appeared in the Ottawa Journal last night, a newspaper which is notoriously not unfriendly to hon. gentlemen opposite. This situation gives us all cause for concern, because the money, after all, comes out of our pockets. I think that generally speaking we have got value for our money up to now, but we will still have to pay whether we get value or not, and if we have to pay an unnecessary amount because the cream is skimmed off in this field by private stations importing material from the outside, as would appear to be the implication of the granting of this Ottawa licence to this particular licencee, it seems to me it is a cause for very grave concern indeed.
I should like very much to put on the record, though I do not think I will, a letter written by another notorious "Liberal" in this country, and I use the word ironically, Mr. Joseph Sedgewick, Q.C. of Toronto, which appeared on March 29 in the Globe and Mail about the granting of the television licence in Toronto. It is entitled "The Curtain Falls". It is true that Mr. Sedgewick was associated with one of the disappointed applicants, and it is true that he was no doubt biased by that

Supply-C.B.C.
view, but I do think that his letter, which I commend to the attention of hon. members, raises almost as many questions as I have raised in what I have had to say here this afternoon. I would say that this is not the kind of thing we expected when the Broadcasting Act was passed and when the board of broadcast governors was established.
I could do as some hon. members have done. I could make a biographical analysis of the board of broadcast governors. I do not intend to do so. That has already been done. I associate myself with my hon. friend from Laurier. I impute no blame to any individual. I know this was a corporate decision, presumably made by a majority, but in the case of Toronto I have no hesitation about saying it was a bad and a wrong decision. In the case of Ottawa I do not go beyond saying that the implications of that decision are, I think, very frightening for anybody who agrees about maintaining at reasonable cost to the Canadian people the Canadian content and character of our television broadcasting.

About a month ago when we set up the committee on broadcasting we had a debate which covered much of this ground. I have thought a bit in the interim about whether it is worth crying over spilt milk. The decision of the board of broadcast governors in the major areas has been taken. Most of us dislike these decisions-
Who? Who dislikes them?
I would say that most of us who are likely to speak here do.
I doubt that. Are you speaking for yourself, or for whom?

Let me put it this way: in any case, our party dislikes them, and I think the decision with regard to Toronto was, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate says, wrong and bad.
The minister when he was speaking on June 21 referred to innuendo and indicated that he wanted the people who are prepared to make these charges against the board of broadcast governors to make them and not hide behind excuses. I assume by that the minister wanted to see this question come before the broadcasting committee. I think he is a fair man in that regard, and I think he knows we are not going to have anything of that kind this session. I can just imagine what that would involve at the present time, with the long hours we are sitting, to have Mr. Bassett or Mr. Hendrick or Mr. Sedge-wick appear before the committee in order that we may hear the views of the board of broadcast governors. I assume we should

have to call people like that in order to bring the board of governors into focus.
The minister raised a question of innuendo. That is the standard reply to anyone who is going on sketchy information, and I admit the information is sketchy. I could give the minister a long parade of how the whole Bassett thing came up. For instance, I remember a Telegram reporter saying in reply to some joshing I was giving him about the gaudy way they were painting the Prime Minister: Well, wait until we get the television licence and we shall see the way it straightens out. That is, in essence, gossip, but this is about the only way we can make an appreciation of all the facets, and there have been many things said about the Telegram application, not only by rival newspapers such as the Star and the Globe. Public opinion in general has been outraged by the way this was awarded. I have heard a story that the vote was eight to four among the members of the board. That is another one that is going around. We are prepared to say that the award has been made and that there is no possibility of rescinding it, but we should like to know more from the board of broadcast governors both at this time and later when it comes before the committee about the reason why it had evaluated things in that way.
I think it has been pointed out by many people that there have been marked inconsistencies in the awards. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has found a little principle in that newspapers should not be given the licences. Anyone looking at the attitude of newspapers throughout the years toward the mediums first of radio and then television will discover that the newspapers decided that if you cannot lick them you should join them or buy them out. The process goes on. I see that Thomson was given the right to buy into the North Bay station.
The book entitled "The History of Journalism" sets out resolutions passed throughout the years in Canada by newspapers with respect to radio. A reading of it reveals that early in the game they decided to buy into the radio racket as soon as they could and they did. The newspapers own many radio stations. The question is, has the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate a new principle in so far as television is concerned?
Obviously the principle was well breached during the Liberal administration-perhaps, as the hon. gentleman said, not from a Liberal point of view-but it was breached. With the concentration of ownership in these media the trend is obvious. You have only to look at Thomson to see it. Obviously the question now is this: should it become a hard and

fast principle and should the board decide to try and get the licences now controlled by newspapers into different hands?
Another principle involved in the Toronto, Halifax and Ottawa applications was whether a radio station has any prior right to a television licence or should it be considered the same way as a newspaper? In Halifax a radio station got it. In Ottawa a radio station was turned down. In Toronto several radio stations were turned down. No inkling as to the principle involved can be taken from the experience in those communities.
We feel that ownership by a radio station of a television station is less dangerous. There are some technical and programming similarities which make it advantageous rather than the contrary. We would like to have the board's view on this matter.
If we are going to have the board before us next year we would like to see a review in the board of broadcast governors' annual report or some other report available to the committee of the way the board went about reaching its decisions. There is a new prospect now looming on the horizon. In a small area just as much trouble can be caused through the establishment of additional television stations. I can tell the board that if it decides to entertain applications for another television station in the Port Arthur-Fort William area there will be just as fierce a controversy as took place in Toronto. The only difference is that it will be on a smaller scale. We want to know what the ground rules are in so far as these other stations in the smaller cities are concerned.
One ground rule I want to know about in particular involves the market, the size, the economics of the matter, from the B.B.G. point of view. With Telemeter going into some smaller places with one television station on the market and with a number of competing broadcasting stations it seems to me almost fantastic to expect that another television station will make money. Yet there is a great logic in having it. If, as hon. members of the government remind us, this is a free enterprise economy it is logical that we give other people a chance, throw the competition open. We should know more about this aspect of the board's future plans.
Even more than in the awarding of licences this group is interested in another aspect of the board's endeavours. Everyone was critical of the C.B.C. in its role as supervisor-that is not the right word and perhaps it would be more accurate to describe its role as program regulator-of private interests so far as content of programs is concerned. I understand that the board did not take over many of the employees of the C.B.C. who
Supply-C.B.C.
were working in this field. I understand they have hired Ross McLean as one of their employees and his chore is to check logs and supervise programs-again I use that word in its special sense-so the board will have an appreciation of what the stations are doing. We need to know how they are moving in this field.
I want to know about the CKLW situation. When the act was passed it allowed those stations which had foreign ownership to continue in that way. I do not think we would have been prepared to pass that section of the act if we had known that the foreign share of the ownership was not going te be stabilized. As I understand it the foreign ownership of CKLW has increased since the act was passed. This station must derive a great deal of its revenue from the United States market in order to continue. In the Toronto area complaints are constantly being made about Buffalo stations coming into the Canadian market. Recently Saturday Night carried a flattering article about the relationship between Time magazine and the Prime Minister and the whole set-up of revenues for Canadian publications.
Here again a Canadian station is raiding a United States area for revenue. I know that the Americans will not worry about it because it is probably only a pinprick in relation to the total market area but the principle is still the same. Here is a Canadian station, both radio and television, licensed through Canadian authorities and operating on Canadian soil, catering to and getting much of its advertising revenue from the United States side of the line. I understand that the board has looked into the matter. I want to know what its views are with respect to that station and its operation.
I have had a number of complaints from the Windsor area about the fact that the news broadcasters on Windsor programs are American and that most of the orientation is in that direction. If we have a bi-national community there there may be some excuse but as I understand it this is a radio and television station licensed and operating in Canada. Despite the fact that the act allows foreign ownership to run it I cannot see why it should compete in the United States market and why it should carry what in essence are United States programs.
There are a number of other examples. Some of the private stations in Canadian television have done a tremendous job in local service programming. I think of Sault Ste. Marie and Timmins. In those communities I have had an opportunity of visiting the studios and watching the programs. These communities are offered many hours of

Supply-C.B.C.
local programming each week. There is a great effort made to make the station stand for something in each of those communities. But what do we get in other places? I can tell the minister about a station close to my home where the local programming is practically non-existent. This situation has been going on for two and a half years. The C.B.C. did not do anything about it. What will the board of broadcast governors do about it? The action it takes in this field will be proof to me whether the board of broadcast governors will function and operate in the long run. In the short run I appreciate that the board has been faced with dirty and difficult decisions about licences. I could get as worked up about that subject as anyone else but in the long run its performance will be judged on its regulating role and whether it does it fairly and honestly. Of course, we will watch for the 55 per cent Canadian content and that type of thing.
The board has been in existence long enough that we should now have some indication of correction and adjustment and letters to show cause why licences could not be rescinded when obviously the stations are not living up to the code. I know that the argument will be to the effect that the board has already held hearings such as that. I want to know about the concrete results of the hearings. It does not do any good to slap private broadcasters on the wrist and say, "Naughty, naughty". You have to be tougher than that. This is what the B.B.G. is to do.
I remember people complaining to the C.B.C. about a local station that used to have 15 or 20 spots in one hour, quite against the law. The people would write to the C.B.C. complaining about this and the C.B.C. would send the station a letter but that was all that was done. The station continued with its over-crowding of spots. That is just one small example. The board is faced with a role we would like to see it carry out with justice but with fairness and thoroughness and in accordance with the rules and regulations set up. At the present time we do not know whether it is going to do better than the C.B.C.
I have been disappointed that the board has not given any indication that it is going to take a lead in setting up regulations that will encourage educational and school broadcasting. We have the likelihood of a private network. I understand the board is encouraging private television networks. It is going to set general regulations in regard to it but I think we are

lagging badly behind in educational television in Canada, and all the excuses of provincial jurisdiction do not answer the question. This is a medium that we need to use in the educational field and unless the board is willing to give some kind of leadership through regulation we will not have it.
One of the aspects the board has already touched on is unsatisfactory to us, and that is their notice issued on March 31, 1959 in relation to political and controversial broadcasting. There are a number of points in this that are ambiguous. I can give one right here in relation to controversial broadcasting and also governing purchase of time. It makes a whole host of qualifications that to me would just end the possibility of controversial broadcasting of any kind. One of the points I cannot understand is why if someone comes in with a partisan controversial broadcast the station must give time to the other person to answer. This is in the United States tradition, but nothing is said in the regulations about the question of payment. Does the person who gets the chance to rebut have to pay? If not, why not? What about the matter of equal time or comparative time? It seems to me that the eight points under controversial broadcasting are almost useless because some of them are ambiguous and the others are far too restraining. Take point No. 7 as an example. It reads:
The broadcast must be of sufficient Interest to the public to justify inclusion in the program schedule.
Who is going to make that judgment? Of course, the board of broadcast governors and the local area, the local station such as Port Arthur, Timmins, Sault Ste Marie or North Bay. Can you see the possibility of a controversial program of local or regional interest that has to go through all the rigmarole of being cleared by the board of broadcast governors? It does not make sense to me, and yet it is one of the ways in which television can play its part, by allowing controversial broadcasting supporting various points of view. I do not mean political, I mean organizational, or economic, that type of thing.
As a matter of fact, I can tell the chairman of the board that these rules are already being broken. I know of a number of places where controversial broadcasting is taking place, being sponsored in various areas, and there is no clearance with the board of broadcast governors, and no approval is sought. This proves to me that these eight points are largely inapplicable.
The final point I wanted to touch on in general, Mr. Chairman, was to ask the minister to give us an explanation through the board

of their views and the action they took in relation to a letter put out by W. W. Williams, president and general manager of the Proctor and Gamble Company of Canada, Limited and dated September 17, 1959. This letter was addressed to Mr. W. A. Johnston, Q.C., Red River television association, Winnipeg, Manitoba. I wish to read one paragraph and to know what action the board took as a result of finding the existence of this paragraph in a brief which was presented to it. The paragraph reads:
I am, of course, implying that the board of broadcast governors' proposed regulations may seriously damage the economic health of the television broadcasting business; and I, therefore, believe that it is vitally in your interest to put up, individually or through C.A.B., the strongest possible fight against the B.B.G.'s proposals. And in this respect I can assure you that through A.C.A. and through our contracts with C.A.B. directors, this company is devoting a great deal of time and energy to the task of helping independent broadcasters to ward off this major threat to their economic well-being.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Will the hon. member indicate the date of the letter?

September 17, 1959. I was just asked the date of the letter. Hon. members may consider that this is water over the bridge. In some ways it may be, but if this view of the board of broadcast governors and what it is set up to do represents the honest reaction of most of the larger advertisers of this country it seems to me that we may have a continuing difficulty so far as the respect given to the board of broadcast governors by the private broadcasting stations is concerned, who in the main will be very much influenced by their advertising revenue. This is the kind of letter that Mr. Williams may regret having written.
He did.

But I certainly think we should know how the board reacted to this specific example.
I would imagine that not too long after the new private stations get going in the metropolitan areas the 55 per cent program content rule is really going to hurt in so far as the opportunity to maximize revenue is concerned. The tradition in so far as the past record of the broadcasting stations is concerned is that when they are vying for a licence they will promise very much-they are like politicians to a degree in that way -and then when they are going along through the course of their administration the promises can be forgotten. They are not in as tough a position as the politician. The politician does have to go back to the electorate. All the broadcasting stations have to do is to go back to the C.B.C. and now to the B.B.G. I should like to think that the
Supply-C.B.C.
B.B.G. is going to be as tough on the broadcasters as the electorate have been on the politicians and their promises.
It seems to me that this particular regulation is the heart of the attempt, the continuing attempt-and I will give credit to this government for the continuing attempt-to keep Canadian broadcasting Canadian in character.
The question raised by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate about Granada Film introduces another element into the question of Canadianism. I took it from his remarks that he feels there is nothing intrinsically valuable in material from British sources.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think the hon. member wants to put words in my mouth. I said no such thing, implied no such thing and meant no such thing; but I do not think we want to turn our Canadian broadcasting over to any other country except Canada.
You never will with this government.

Granada Film is a very successful organization in Great Britain. It seems to me they will have available for this particular station, and probably for this private network, a very great deal in the way of film. I should like to know from the board what the views are on the relationship of British material to Canadian content. I know they have already given it, but in the light of those developments, which may mean that we get much more British material than perhaps we can stand, in the light of our general Canadianism, is the board prepared to make an adjustment? What are its views if we should be subject to a flood of British films? I personally do not think it is likely to come about because most Canadians will find that British fare is pretty limited to their taste.
I see the hon. member for Kootenay West looking around, and realizing that the sturdy yeomanry in Kootenay West have a different appreciation of this sort of thing than the Canadians in my part of the country, probably I should conclude here by saying that we gave very serious consideration, just as a gesture of disapproval, to moving that the estimates of the board of broadcast governors be reduced to one dollar. We thought this would underline our dissatisfaction with the way the board has gone about awarding these licences. However, in the long run, in view of the fact we desire to get through with this matter as quickly as possible, we decided to let that procedural flourish go and just re-emphasize our concern over the awards

Supply-C.B.C.
that have been made and our interest in finding out more about why they are made and how the future is going to go.
I should like to repeat that we would very much like to have some evidence that the board of broadcast governors is not going to pat private broadcasters on the wrist but that occasionally they are going to punch them on the nose.

I should like to speak very briefly on these estimates for the board of broadcast governors. I should like to say, particularly in the light of what has been said this afternoon, that I want to pay a well deserved tribute to the board of broadcast governors for doing an excellent job under most difficult circumstances. The hon. member for Port Arthur did not put it quite that way. He said, a difficult and dirty job. I do not believe it is a dirty job. I think they have brought a new sense of honour to the industry and they are doing an excellent job.
If we were to follow the argument of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate then the board of broadcast governors would have no alternative but to immediately preclude two of the most capable, most knowledgeable groups in this country from the television industry. I am thinking of those people who are associated with the newspaper business and those people who are considered to be Conservatives.

I am sure the hon. gentleman does not want to misrepresent what I said. I never took the slightest exception to anyone who is a Conservative being granted a licence. I pointed out that we gave a licence to the London Free Press, a notoriously Conservative newspaper.
I think you will find that was the only television licence that went to anybody who was known as a Conservative.

What about Thomson?
Perhaps the hon. gentleman should learn a little history.

All I can say is this: When the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate gets up moaning and groaning, as he has been, about the skulduggery that went on in Toronto in connection with the application for a T.V. licence in that area, he perhaps ought to bear in mind that one of the directors connected with the successful applicant is Mr. Joel Aldred. I might say that Mr. Aldred counts amongst his many personal friends Premier Smallwood of Newfoundland. I am sure that, on reflection, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate would not want to leave a wrong impression about his views on this matter.
As I said, the board of broadcast governors is comprised of very capable people from all walks of life in Canada. They have received praise and approval from the broadcasting industry, including the private broadcasters. Perhaps if the hon. member made himself familiar with the literature put out by the private broadcasters he would become aware of this fact. Then, too, the C.B.C. approves of the board of broadcast governors which is doing an excellent job under most difficult circumstances.
In conclusion I would say as a private member of this house, if there is one thing this government has done that we can look to with pride, it is the forward looking legislation on broadcasting and the establishment of the board of broadcast governors.

I rise to speak very briefly on a matter of local concern. I shall not range into the wider field of the functions of the board of broadcast governors because I think that has been very well covered by other speakers. I do want to make a suggestion to the minister and the board of broadcast governors. While the responsibility for certifying the suitability of equipment for these small satellite television broadcasting stations rests on the telecommunications branch of the Department of Transport, the responsibility for actually granting licences to operate is, I understand, that of the board of broadcast governors.
This matter is of some importance to the people in the Kootenay district and, no doubt, in other country areas, who are denied the opportunity of receiving the usual television programs because of the physical features of the surrounding country. These small community satellite television stations, therefore, are absolutely necessary if a number of people in isolated places are to obtain any television at all. I understand that has been the experience of a number of districts throughout Canada.
I am informed that at the present time there are a number of these community satellite broadcasting stations operating under the ownership of small incorporated local companies, some under co-operative societies and some owned by individuals. I find, upon inquiry, that they are performing a very good service for these small communities practically on a non-profit basis. The suggestion I want to make, and I make it as a result of some experience with two or three groups who have been trying to establish community stations of this type, concerns the publication of a small pamphlet.
These groups often lack experience, a knowledge of the law and regulations, which

leads to wasted effort, misunderstandings and things of that sort. I am quite sure that as more and more people find out about the success of some of these stations operating in other districts they will want to obtain television for their areas. I simply make the suggestion that it would be a good idea if the board of broadcast governors published a small manual containing information with respect to application procedures, with respect to the certification of equipment by the telecommunications branch of the Department of Transport, and the general principles upon which the board of broadcast governors acts when examining applications for these licences. This information could be given to these groups as a result of the experience of the officials in the telecommunications branch and the experience in the administrative aspects of the situation of the board of broadcast governors. I make that suggestion because I think something could be done in that way to assist these people in more readily obtaining what they require, what they are entitled to, without a waste of effort or, in some cases, a waste of money.

There is one further point I wish to raise that relates to something completely separate from anything else I have said. It relates to what is, in effect, perhaps an apology. When the matter first came up on June 21 I was speaking about the Toronto application and making a point about the Toronto Telegram application. Someone shouted, what about the Star. Just in passing, I said, well everyone knows that the Star's is not a serious application, or words to that effect. The Star has supplied me with a full transcript of their proposals and their rebuttals, and in fairness I should say this was a serious application.
What I really did have in my mind when I made that passing remark about the seriousness of the application was that the Star was forced into making an application because the Telegram was feet first into the field. In that sense they felt and I believe that they admitted before the hearings that they had been primarily interested in the licence but that in order to protect themselves they felt they should get into the field and make an application and in order to make their application as pointed as possible and as consistent with their principles which had been against this marriage of television and newspapers, they were prepared to set up their station ownership on a basis that would be of a non-profit kind and that any incomes or revenues above the cost aspect would go into some kind of foundation, as I understand it. Therefore any comment that it was not a serious application was unfair to the time and
Supply-C.B.C.
the effort that the Star put into trying to put forward both a kind of programming and an ownership that they thought would appeal to the board. I should like to apologize if in that scant remark I did the Star an injustice. In using those words I should not like it to be read that I would have liked to see the Toronto Star get the licence, although relatively perhaps the Star over the Telegram and perhaps relatively the Globe over the Star but preferably no newspaper should get a television licence.

I shall take only a few minutes of the time of the committee, with the committee's permission. I am, of course, in the hands of the committee. Naturally we will deal with any points that are raised but I think most of them are within very short compass. In starting out, the hon. member for Laurier read the statement of Lord Bennett with respect to the principles which should govern the allocation of the air. He said that the air was in the public domain. I agree with that statement entirely and so does the government. I am sure that the board of broadcast governors in all of its actions have shown that they accept that principle and that they have carried it out.
I should perhaps deal with these things seriatum. I understood the hon. member for Laurier to refer particularly to the Ottawa station as being under foreign control or at least I think he said 33J per cent of it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I said "outside capital", which is different.

Yes, outside capital. I inferred this from what he said. If he did not intend it, then I am sure he will correct me. From what he said I gathered that the outside capital was going to be in control of the corporation and there was much reference to Granada and N.T.A. telefilms and there have been many rumours floating around from every disappointed applicant. Every one of them, of course, feels that he was the one who should have had the laying on of hands, that he was the one who was especially favoured by heaven or by God or whatever it may be and that he was the one who should have had the application granted to him and that everyone else was defected, mentally, financially or in some other way. There have been a great many biased stories told about this Ottawa situation. I received a letter the other day from a disappointed applicant pointing out that there was foreign control here and a great many other matters, most of which are entirely baseless.
The act makes it plain that there can be no more than 25 per cent of the shares owned by anyone outside of Canada. That is the

Supply-C.B.C.
fundamental principle. If the hon. member for Laurier said something about 33J per cent, as I gather he did, or as I recall it although I did not mark it down at the time, then obviously he was misinformed on the matter.
The hon. member also referred to the voting trust and suggested there was something sinister about that voting trust and that there was again outside foreign control. May I say this about the voting trust. All this, of course, was disclosed in evidence. All this was sworn to. I wonder how many of these critics attended any hearings, how many of them read the briefs or how many of them read the evidence or how many of them have seen or watched the briefs being presented and then are prepared to come in here and criticize.
One of the most shocking things I have heard in the years I have been in this House of Commons is the casual statement made by our good natured friend the hon. member for Port Arthur who said that they seriously considered moving to reduce this vote to a dollar; he was not sure about the amount. As I said earlier, he has always had dissatisfaction, worries, cares, misapprehensions and suspicion. But the thought of responsible men and women who are taking part in a public service in this country, many of them at great sacrifice and the thought that moving to reduce the estimates would be a casual matter is something that I cannot understand. I cannot conceive of anything more insulting to the board or anything that would show greater irresponsibility than any such action. Perhaps he was only being facetious and I hope that was the case. However, if that was intended as a serious step, it is one which I think is a reflection on those who consider that course of action and is one which is absolutely unwarranted by the facts.
May I ask the minister a question?
Yes.

Is it not a fact that one way of showing dissatisfaction in this house with the performance of any organization that comes before the house with estimates is to make such a motion? We have expressed our dissatisfaction with the board. What could be more natural than that we should consider this course? I told the minister we decided not to do it.

The hon. member has not expressed dissatisfaction with the board. He expressed some rumours. He fears. He suffers from apprehension. I do not know how he can sleep at night. He suffers from his dreams, hallucinations and worries. Not one word has been said this afternoon by him or
[Mr. Nowlan.l
by anyone else except what was based on rumours, and 90 per cent of the rumours are false.
There was a reference to the voting trust. If there was any misunderstanding on that, I do not know what my hon. friend's information is with respect to the voting trust. There is a voting trust. As disclosed in the evidence, it was to keep control here in Ottawa. There are three trustees, namely Mr. Ted Beament who was solicitor for the applicant. Mr. Landriault and Mr. Bushnell. Those are three Canadian trustees residing in Ottawa. The trustees would be here within this company. This is the break-down of stock. We have heard about N.T.A. Telefilms, a dreadful thing, of a United States firm coming in to take control, Granada to take control. According to them we are really faced with a disaster.
This is what was sworn to in evidence and this is what I am advised by the officials again today, namely that Granada and N.T.A. Telefilms together own 24.9 per cent of the voting shares and that the other 75.1 per cent are owned by Canadians. In connection with this Ottawa company, as with all the other companies which have been approved by the board, there has not been more than 25 per cent of the shares owned by people outside of Canada nor can there be under the act. The board has made that matter abundantly plain and has inquired into every applicant. There is the sworn evidence there as to the financial breakdown and everything else.
I know my hon. friend would not mislead the House of Commons under any circumstances but I think that possibly he has obtained some misinformation, as many other people do, from biased people who have been disappointed and who make rumour for fact. The recent decisions of the board, the Ottawa decision and the Halifax decision, have not yet been approved by the governor in council. There is all sorts of political pressure being exerted and propaganda being spread in the hope of influencing the government to repudiate the decision of the board in this matter.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question?
Certainly. Whether or not I can answer it, I do not know.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am sure the minister does not want to misrepresent what I said. When he started to reply he used the words "sinister agreement". I took it down. I think he will have to look very carefully into the blues and into anything I said which would indicate the use of those words. I did not use it. I said that I had been informed there was an agreement to the effect and so on. The minister

has replied in part to what I said and I would like to ask him this question. Is it so that each of the shareholders of the Ottawa television company have abandoned their right to their one share and transferred it in favour of the voting trust?

I cannot definitely answer that question, but I do know that on sworn evidence which is a matter of record whatever they may have transferred to these trustees was disclosed to the board in every way, shape and form and there is no possibility, unless someone has committed perjury, in which case the situation can be easily rectified because the board has disciplinary powers-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I be permitted to intervene here. I thank the minister for the explanation but if it is the fact that each shareholder has transferred his right to his vote in favour of the voting trust, then it changes the position which the minister has explained very materially.

I do not follow that. There are three local residents in Ottawa who constitute the voting trust and full details of it were disclosed to the board. A careful examination was made with respect to it, but the fact still remains that the shares are owned by Canadians with the exception of 24.9 per cent which are divided between the U.S. company and Granada. I am informed again this afternoon, so that there is no question in anyone's mind listening to the debate today, that the control of this firm rests entirely in Canadian hands, with the one exception of the 24.9 per cent. I am sure that is the situation.
The hon. member for Laurier referred to the practices which used to be carried on in his department when he was minister, and either he or the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate asked me to outline briefly the procedure followed in dealing with these applications. I do not think there is anything different from the days when the hon. gentleman presided over the Department of Transport. As he knows, the applicant has to make application to the Department of Transport. There is a large file of correspondence and documents, and ultimately after many consultations and much study the officials of the Department of Transport approve, if they do, the technical phases of the application.
Then that having been done and upon D.O.T. advising the board of broadcast governors that it is clear technically-I am not quite sure of the chronological order-perhaps the two can proceed together to appoint-the applicant appears before the B.B.G. and has
Supply-C.B.C.
to file his brief, the advertisements and all the documents in relation thereto. Ultimately the board of broadcast governors holds a hearing.
There is a slight deviation now because of the fact that we do have the B.B.G., although under the act the Minister of Transport is responsible for the technical clearing of it and under the Radio Act that has not changed. Then when it comes from the board I, as Minister of National Revenue having been designated by order in council as the minister to whom the B.B.G. reports, present the board's recommendation to the cabinet where it is dealt with by the government and then an order in council is issued and the mechanics of the whole transaction are then complete.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: One question which I asked was whether the Ottawa recommendation had been approved by the government and what other of these six or eight applications had not.

I am coming to that. The Ottawa application has not been approved by the governor in council; it has not yet been submitted to him. As the hon. member knows, it takes some time. Having the background necessary he would know it usually takes a few weeks from the time it goes to D.O.T.
I should have said that after the hearing the report follows to D.O.T. and the technical documents concerning the granting of the licence are prepared in D.O.T. and they then come to me. They have come forward but I have not yet presented that application to the cabinet, nor have I the one for Ottawa, nor have I the one for Edmonton. They are the three, plus the one at Pembroke, which are still outstanding.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: All the others have been recommended?

Halifax, Ottawa, Edmonton and the one at Pembroke. They are the television applications which have been recommended, and my parliamentary secretary says that there is the Calgary one too in the background which has not come forward yet.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He would not know about the Edmonton one.
There has been a lot of pressure on the cabinet. With the house sitting in the morning the hours are very short and it has not yet been dealt with. I think that clears up the mechanics of the matter.

Perhaps the minister has forgotten but I asked him a question which he said he would prefer to answer at this time concerning C.B.C. applications, which of course never went to the board in our

Supply-C.B.C.
day. I asked him to give us the ABC of where they originated. What I am interested in is the point at which the government decides.

The situation there is exactly the same as that of other applicants. The C.B.C., if it desires to make application, has to get that application cleared by the Department of Transport so far as the technical aspects are concerned. It has probably already made an application. I am not sure what the schedule is but I presume they make application hoping that D.O.T. clears it, and then after D.O.T. gives clearance it comes to the board of broadcast governors to be heard. The same procedure as I outlined a moment ago is then followed.
I know what the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate has in mind because he suggested it very forcibly the other day. I am prepared to go along with him on the fact that there is a difficult area there, one which was certainly not foreseen when the act was drafted. Whether or not something should be done with that, I agree it is rather unfair to have private applicants making application at the same time as publicly owned applicants, particularly if the publicly owned one gets the application in the end.
We must all remember here that the C.B.C. also applied for Pembroke in the same way as it applied for Edmonton. True, Edmonton is a big oyster and Pembroke a relatively small one, but the B.B.G. refused the application of the C.B.C. for Pembroke and granted it to a private firm, but did approve of the C.B.C. application for Edmonton. I must say that I was the most surprised man in the world when that happened, but there was certainly no understanding whatsoever about it in any way, shape or form.
From the suggestions we have heard this afternoon it is amazing how many conflicting viewpoints one can get if you want to build up a case. I have heard suggestions of political rewards this afternoon, political rewards in connection with Halifax, Toronto and Ottawa. If there are any political rewards which could be recognized, if this board is an organization which considers politics at all, I cannot conceive of any applicant who might be more deserving than some of the applicants in Edmonton in view of their records of service and co-operation with the Conservative party throughout the years. So if there is any merit in the argument about politics entering into this thing then I should think that argument is shot pretty badly by the board's decision that the Edmonton application should be granted to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I can assure hon. members opposite that there are probably
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
quite a few staunch Conservatives in and around the city of Edmonton who, to say the least, would not express any paeans of praise about this board, and if they thought there should have been political recognition and they found that there was not I suspect that their expressions of loyalty and devotion would be more pleasing to the ears of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate than to my own.

I would like to ask a question at this point. As the minister has pointed out to the hon. member for Laurier in the case of the Ottawa station, a private applicant has to satisfy the B.B.G. that he has the financial competence to carry out and perform. Now surely the minister is not telling us, as he seems to be, that the C.B.C. can blithely make an application to the
B.	B.G. without satisfying the B.B.G. that it has the financial competence to carry it out? It has no financial competence until it has a categorical, unqualified assurance from the government that if it gets the licence the government is prepared to put up the money. That is the whole point, and I have never been able to get it straight up to now. I ask the minister with respect to this Edmonton station: did the government give this assurance to the C.B.C. before they made that application that the money would be made available before they got the licence?

Categorically, the answer to that is, no. There was no discussion between the government and the C.B.C. with respect to that application. It was only after that application was made-I do not know how many days later-that the president of the
C.	B.C. informed me in conversation that he had made an application for this Edmonton licence. It was included in the capital budget of the C.B.C. which had been passed months before. There was a fairly substantial item there which would cover any expenditure which would be needed this year under capital development. I am told that the chairman of the board of broadcast governors asked the C.B.C. if they had enough money available, and the board was told they had sufficient moneys in their budget to proceed with the expenditure which would be necessary this year. That is the situation with respect to that.

May I ask a further supplementary question about that? This, in view of the treasury control which the minister has told us exists, does seem to me to suggest that the board of broadcast governors was either naive indeed, or taking parliament for granted. I return to this fundamental point: surely it is shockingly unfair

to private applicants who come into this competition with the C.B.C. without an absolutely clear knowledge of whether in fact the government really intends to put up the money.

The chairman tells me that he was advised by the C.B.C. that they had the money. No specific reference was made to the estimates, but in reply to questions asked by the board when the president of the C.B.C. was before the board the information was given that funds were available. I perhaps interpreted it by saying, as I found out afterwards, that there was an item in the estimates which would be large enough to cover the expenditures for this year and it was on that the C.B.C. based the information they gave the board.

Did the board give any consideration to the fact that the money spent by the C.B.C. in a capital sense upon the Edmonton station might be money which could be used to expand the television service there? I understood that this was part of the board's role as leader in this field.

I am not sure whether the board made inquiries on that score or not. I assume they did. The chairman has just indicated to me that they did make such an inquiry. They would be very properly told by the C.B.C. that the moneys available for this year were such that the acquisition of this licence would not interfere with other extensions which the C.B.C. planned to put into operation. Perhaps this should be pointed out: there has been a great deal of talk here-perhaps I would be saying the same thing if I were sitting in some other place-to the effect that this spending of money in Edmonton was showing neglect of the back areas, the rural communities. A superficial case could perhaps be made out on that basis. However, it should be borne in mind that the C.B.C. has no transmitting facilities between Winnipeg and Vancouver. If this is to be a national system, then certainly the corporation needs transmission facilities somewhere on the prairies over this vast expanse of 2,000 miles, and Alberta was the logical place where such facilities should go.
In addition to that, the internal estimates of the C.B.C., which are usually fairly accurate, proved conclusively to the corporation that the expenditures in Edmonton could be recovered entirely and financed on an amortization basis because the commercial revenues would be more than sufficient to carry the financial load imposed on the corporation. That is a position entirely different from that which exists in these outlying rural areas where the corporation has to operate and
Supply-C.B.C.
where, I agree, it should operate. But the corporation has to get money either from the government or from its own revenues in order to carry out these extensions, and the argument which the C.B.C. would make, if you were sitting around the table with their officials and having a friendly discussion on this matter, is that by getting this station in Edmonton and its commercial revenues they would be able to extend their facilities in the rural areas more rapidly than would otherwise be the case. I may add that a substantial representation came to appear before the board of broadcast governors from the rural areas in the province of Alberta with a view to opposing the application, but when the argument of the C.B.C. had been explained to them they turned round and supported the C.B.C.'s case before the board. Thus, those who came to scoff remained to pray.
I do not wish to detain hon. members for too long this afternoon. They have already spent a great deal of time here and, in fact, I would not mind getting out myself, but the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate raised the question of newspaper control. He deprecated it, and I think that on philosophic grounds I would be inclined to agree with him. But he produced enough examples of what had happened in the past to show that there was no fixed pattern. Indeed, if there was a pattern it showed that newspapers did receive licences, whether there was one applicant or not. We do not know all the factors which existed in those days-

The minister says we do not know all the factors that existed, but I spent a great deal of time in finding out what those factors were.
