They are very well known; they are all in the records of the old board of the C.B.C., and I asserted that in all the cases mentioned in the Toronto Telegram, except one, as far as I could find the station connected with the newspaper was the only applicant. In one case there was one other applicant.

I am not questioning that for a moment. But how did they get one applicant? What pressures went on up to that point? This was years ago, and the fact that there was only one applicant means nothing today. The fact remains that under the previous government newspapers were awardee' television licences. I am not saying that was wrong, but I do say it shows a blind sense of criticism to criticize this board-the board, not the government, because the government has had nothing to do with this board in any way especially with regard to any of these applications; I want to make that perfectly clear-when under the former government television licences were granted to newspapers

Supply-C.B.C.
or when, on occasions, T.V. licences were denied which the C.B.C. thought would be awarded to them that principle was established.
There has been a great deal of reference to the Fowler report when it suited hon. gentlemen to quote from it. I wonder if hon. members opposite have read the paragraph in that report dealing with the granting of television licences to newspapers. The following is found at page 109 of the Fowler report:
It is not a matter that should be subject to rigid rules of general application, but should depend on the discretion of the minister and his advisers including the board of broadcast governors.
This was in the old days when the minister had some discretion.
Which he still has. It is exactly the same; there is no change whatever.

He has not. I continue:
The test should be the practical one of ascertaining the best immediate and long term interests of the particular community concerned, rather than the private interests of any of the individual applicants.
With that I quite concur. We find that with the approval of the Fowler commission there is no merit whatsoever in the general proposition that newspapers should not be entitled to receive a television licence. I would be inclined to agree with the hon. member though, and would personally deprecate the assemblage of too much power, information or propaganda-call it what you will-in the hands of any one group whether it be newspaper people, television people or anyone else.
I think I have dealt sufficiently with the matter of the Ottawa application. There have been references to Toronto and to the fact that there were some unsatisfactory matters there. There were rumours of some kind to the effect that someone had said he had it in the bag. That statement has been denied since. I do not know what anyone has said about having it in the bag but I know he did not have it in the bag because, as I said a moment ago, I am the minister who reports for the board of broadcast governors and I am the only connecting link between the government and the board. Anyone who says that any of those television licences was in the bag is using pure rumour and simple propaganda and such statements are completely without foundation in any way, shape or form.
In one case it was said we made a political payoff in Toronto, rewarding a politician. Who were we rewarding in Ottawa? What is this pay off thing in Ottawa? There was the myth about United States control which we

have exploded, a terrible thing. Statements about political control are without foundation. As I said you would not dare stand on the street in Edmonton and say that there has been any political control over the board of broadcast governors there. I do not think you could convince Grattan O'Leary and the group in Ottawa that there is any political control over the board of broadcast governors. When Dr. Stewart the chairman of the board was first contacted by telephone I remember that a former colleague of mine who is now dead, when I told him I had called Dr. Stewart, made a bet that we would not get him. But, he went on to say, if you get him you will have the best man in Canada. I accepted the judgment of Doctor Sidney Smith then and I am more convinced of it now than ever before.
Dr. Stewart and I talked on the phone and then he came to Ottawa. He said to me, "I have only one question. May I run this thing as I see fit with the assistance of my colleagues or is there to be any political control whatever?" I gave him my assurance that there would be no political influence used on the board in any way, shape or form and to the best of my knowledge and belief there has not been any used from the day the board first sat until today nor will there ever be as long as I, at least, am the minister who reports to parliament for the board of broadcast governors.
Those are the facts of the situation. I do not even know the names of the applicants in Ottawa. I knew that Grattan O'Leary was making an application because I was naturally interested in the activities of an old friend. Ernie Bushnell asked me a year ago whether I thought he should make an application. I told him that he was as free to make as many applications as he liked but that I did not think he would get it. He said, "Have you any influence?" I said, "I have not any influence and I have never attempted to use any but I will tell you frankly, Ernie, if I had any I would use it for Grattan O'Leary rather than for yourself." That is a discussion I had with Ernie Bushnell and those are the facts of the case. The same thing applies to Toronto.
Snide little remarks were made with respect to Halifax, too. The C.C.F. members who are particularly prone in indulging in remarks of this type regard the estimates as something of a joke. The other day the question was asked whether the E. L. Bushnell in Pembroke was the same E. L. Bushnell who had been granted the licence in Ottawa. The other day we also had questions about whether the Finlay MacDonald who was concerned in the application in Halifax was the

same Finlay MacDonald who chaired the Conservative party breakfast at the annual meeting last winter. I am very glad to say that he is exactly the same Finlay MacDonald. I think we of the maritimes put on the best show at that breakfast that was put on in any province in Canada. It is going to be a very sorry day if the mere fact that a man happens to be a Conservative and a good one should result in denying him the right to make an application of this kind.
I think it was my friend the hon. member for Laurier who said that if the application was granted to Finlay MacDonald in Halifax or to the person in Toronto then it was obvious this would be political consideration and would wreck the functions of the board or something of that kind.
Make sure you have it right.
I am only paraphrasing very roughly.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You are paraphrasing very wrongly.

I think that was the inference my hon. friend attempted to take. I jotted down the words the hon. member used and according to my notes the hon. gentleman said that the board would be open to a change of partisanship if the governor in council grants a licence to Ottawa or Toronto applicants according to the report which they now have. As I said, if we are open to a charge of partisanship because the odd Conservative in this country is able because of merit and on the basis of the facts of the situation to achieve some recognition, then it is a sorry day. I do not think hon. members opposite should be too deeply troubled and they should not be heard to say anything critical on this score, either. I have dealt with the applications and the rumours which were baseless.
The hon. member for Port Arthur raised a question about station CKLW and asked whether they were being slapped on the wrist. That is the station at Windsor where the Canadian content of programming is low. The hon. gentleman wanted to know what was being done. I am told by the members of the board who are present that their officials visited that station and communications have been going on between them. It is true that the Canadian content there is low and they have been ordered to increase it. It cannot be done overnight. They have been instructed that there must be a Canadian content of 45 per cent as at the year ending March, 1961 and following that they will have to raise it still further. There is no question in my mind but that when the board slaps you on the wrist you know that you are dealing if not with a mailed fist at 79951-0-393
Supply-C.B.C.
least with a very firm hand. A very firm approach is adopted in any contact there may be with the board.

In connection with that may I ask what the situation is with respect to ownership. I know that this station and the station in Montreal were provided for in terms of foreign control under the act. Is there a range in the amount of foreign ownership?

I can answer that generally, Mr. Chairman. It is true, as the hon. member has said, that the stations in Montreal and Windsor were exempted from the provisions of the act because they had previous licences and so forth. I am told that the Montreal situation has not changed at all, that the ownership is exactly the same as it was. In Windsor, as the hon. member has said, there has been a slight increase in the United States purchase of shares but I am advised that there is no change in the situation, namely that control has always been vested in United States hands. There has been no lack of control as far as the national interest is concerned and I think that is a matter the board is watching very carefully.
There has been some reference to editorial comment in newspapers, some of them biased and some of them disappointed. We have also had references to various articles that have been written. Even these can sometimes be biased. I have known men who were promised jobs by an applicant station and when the applicant station did not get the licence they have been most biased in their writing. Without being too personal let me say that at the moment I can think of an article which has been quoted here today. I know very well why there is the bias and the venom which appears in the article. It is because of the expectations which were perhaps disappointed as a result of the decision which was made.
Certainly, as the hon. member for Port Arthur has said, the newspaper reaction has not been too considerate of the board or the government in recent days since the board of broadcast governors' decision regarding Toronto. The B.B.G., as hon. members know, is planning to conduct studies preparatory to laying down the ground rules for a new network, if a network is justified.
I wish to commend to all hon. members an article on this subject which appears on the editorial page of the Globe and Mail of July 9, 1960 which speaks in most laudatory terms about the board of broadcast governors. After referring to the possible establishment of the new network and the danger arising from domination of the private network by

Supply-C.B.C.
Toronto and Montreal, making it local instead of national in its policy and presentations, the editorial concludes:
The B.B.G. rulings are designed to avoid this; they would spread control across Canada, and so encourage television production across Canada. The B.B.G. is to be applauded for its foresight. It has gone the full distance to ensure that the new network will not only be national, but will serve the national interest.
What date is that?

It is the Globe and Mail of Saturday, July 9, 1960. I think an editorial in such strong language coming from the Globe and Mail, in view of the very objective attitude it has taken towards other matters, is praise which comes almost from Caesar.
There is nothing more that I propose to say except this. As the hon. member for St. John's East said a moment ago, this government-I do not think it has received enough credit for it, not that one looks for credit in this world-has been accused of this and that and the other thing; but there is one pledge we made before we came into power, namely that we were going to separate the C.B.C. as a program organization from one in control of licensing, and so on. We have done that. I think we have done it to the advantage of the C.B.C. I think the C.B.C. is a better organization today because it is divorced from that other responsibility. We brought in the board of broadcast governors. I want to say that to my knowledge, which I think is as great as anybody's in this chamber on this matter because I am getting letters every day, as the hon. member for St. John's East said, the board of broadcast governors has done an excellent job.
I was shocked at the irresponsible proposals considered by the C.C.F. party. I can understand how one can be disappointed, but this board has the confidence of Canadians, and the only ones who are disappointed in it, and they sometimes give expression to their grief among themselves, are those who have failed to get licences. They say, among other things, "We have to be disappointed about it but I am glad you did not get it" and so on. The only ones who are disappointed are those who made applications and have been refused on legitimate grounds.
The great majority of the Canadian people know and realize that this board has done a remarkably good job. This is true of the C.A.B. itself and the private broadcasters. You should hear them express their views about the fairness of the rulings which they say are too tough. They say they are tough but they are fair, and there has never been a sign of partisanship in any action which they have taken. I have had that from a score of members of the C.A.B. who come into my office and discuss these things.

I stand here this afternoon and say that Canada can be very proud of its board of broadcast governors and the fact that we have Canadian citizens like Dr. Stewart and his associates on that board who are prepared to assume the responsibilities that they have assumed, and who deserve some credit and praise, although they never expect to get it, rather than criticism based on misleading rumours and propaganda.

Mr. Chairman, I think the minister would have been much more convincing if he had refrained from the insinuations that he indulged in with respect to the activities of the board of governors of the C.B.C. in the case of the earlier applications. I was surprised that the minister should have said that influence or pressure was brought to bear on applications in the early days of television.

If the hon. member will permit me, I never meant for a moment to reflect on the board of governors of the old C.B.C. He said this was a matter of pressure. If there was pressure it would come from the government and not from the board. I have the highest opinion in the world for the board for which I had the responsibility of reporting for a short time, and I certainly would never say anything to reflect on any of them in any way, shape or form.

The minister said that, I think, and misrepresented very much what I said. The only decision that was made by the previous government, as the minister knows full well, was what place would have public television and what place would have private television and the applications, as the minister himself pointed out to the hon. member for Laurier, came in to the Department of Transport in exactly the same way in those days as they do now. They were forwarded in exactly the same way only they went to the C.B.C. board rather than to the board of broadcast governors.
The plain fact is that, as these records I have on my desk show, in a good many cases where newspapers applied and in some cases where other applicants came forward they were deferred because it was hoped another application would turn up. Very far from rushing these things through when there was only one applicant, every effort was made to see that another applicant would come in any doubtful cases and, notwithstanding that fact, in that list that the Toronto Telegram undertook to produce to refute the argument that I made, they were able to find only one case where there was any other applicant at all that I can discover, and in that case the other applicant was reported by the C.B.C. board to be unsatisfactory.

It does happen that there were, I think, one or two other newspapers that the Toronto Telegram did not get on its list that I happen to see here, and in one of those cases there were two applications and the newspaper got it. I think anybody who would look for two minutes at the information that is given here would see why; but I think that anything that I said from the start in relation to this is not in any way inconsistent with what is in the Fowler report at all.
Of course, one has to take account of all the circumstances and one very important circumstance is that you are not going to give a licence to some fly by night person who has not the capacity to run a station and deny it to a newspaper, or a newspaper publisher, and prevent a locality from having decent television. That, I repeat, was not the case in Toronto. There were nine applicants there, of whom six had no connection with newspapers or no connection that I know of with newspapers. At least there were a considerable number that had none and the board itself, according to the newspaper reports- that is all I have to go on-said they had a hard time distinguishing among the applicants. I feel they should not have considered the three big newspaper applicants. I say again that as a matter of principle I think this was a thoroughly bad decision in the light of the facts as they existed there and quite unprecedented. The minister's attempt to make a precedent out of these other cases falls absolutely flat on its face because in all these other cases there were no other comparable applicants at all.
With respect to the Edmonton case, I must say that I come from Missouri. If two years from now the minister can show me that Edmonton C.B.C. station is making money for the C.B.C. I will apologize to the minister publicly; but I will need a lot of convincing and I will want to go over the figures very carefully, but I hope he is right.

I said 1 was told that by the C.B.C. Certainly it cannot happen in two years because it will take two years probably before the station comes into operation and it would have to be an immensely lucrative station if it starts to pay for itself at the end of six months.
I will give the hon. member two years after it comes into operation.
All right we will make a private bet on it outside. I would like to have a celebration.

I realize that gambling typifies the activities of the present administration but it is something that I do not indulge in; but I do undertake, if two years
79951-0-393J
Supply-C.B.C.
after the Edmonton C.B.C. station comes into operation, the minister succeeds in persuading the Minister of Finance to agree to the approving of this application and allows it to have this money this year, all of which will have to be borrowed, incidentally, at very high interest-I will look at that interest rate, too, in making my computation- but if this station has paid everything, not just the axle grease, but everything else, two years from now I will certainly make a public apology to the minister and I will be astonished. I will say he should not be wasting his time as minister; he should be running the C.B.C.
A good suggestion.

I come back to this other matter which I think is a very much more serious question of principle. I know what the minister has done, as he so often does when he is in tight corners. He spoke philosophically; he would be inclined to agree; but here was a case where you did not have to be philosophical. There was a good practical reason for taking a different course, apart from any other consideration.
Here is a city with a million and a half people-I refer to metropolitan Toronto-and only three newspapers. The concentration of the sources of information is already too great, in my view. Of course, the capital that is required today is so great that it is hard to avoid these concentrations. Here was an opportunity, though, to bring in another independent source of information for the public. Instead of that, it was given to one of the three newspapers and that, in turn, is bound to upset the competitive picture as between those three newspapers. I hold no brief for any of these newspapers. I would have liked to see none of the three get it. While privately, perhaps, this would have been my third choice if I had to choose amongst them, I do not believe it should have been a choice amongst them. I think it was a wrong choice.
There is another matter I should like to mention, and here I must confess I am not properly informed. I understood that at the time these other applications were before the board for the Toronto station there was an application from the station in Hamilton for certain technical changes which would enable the Hamilton station to be more effectively viewed in the Toronto area. I should like to know whether or not the board has made a decision about that and, if not, when they expect to make a decision about that. I should like to say that, speaking for myself, I was really quite shocked to find that every one of the nine applicants opposed the application from Hamilton. I remember,

Supply-C.B.C.
not so many years ago when these people were talking about private enterprise. Here was a case where it was suggested there should be more competition in this field, yet all these applicants publicly opposed the entry of Hamilton into this field.
It does seem to me if we are going to have this competition in television which the government has decided, following the recommendation of the Fowler commission, this gift to one station in Toronto should not be made even more lucrative by preventing effective competition from the only other channel that apparently can reach Toronto at the present time. I do feel we ought to be told about this. The other thing is that I believe the minister ought to tell us, in an authoritative way, just what in fact has been decided by the board, if anything has been decided, about a private television network.

I am advised by the board, Mr. Chairman, that the decision has not yet been rendered on the Hamilton application. There were technical problems so the board referred the matter back to the Department of Transport before the board can make a decision.

I was pleased to have one assurance from the minister that the board would not be just patting wrists. I am concerned, in the light of that, at the number of employees the board has for 1960-61. According to the estimates, when you take away all the Indian chiefs, there are not many people left to look after the checking. I wonder if the check is only to be a log check or does the board plan to have a more thorough, occasional spot check on the ground of these various stations.
The other thing I should like to know is, are the services of the audience research division of the C.B.C. going to be used? It does seem to me that if the board is going to be the regulatory master of these stations, especially these new stations, this is a very small staff with which to do an adequate job. I should like to have some more details on that particular point. I should like to know also from the minister something about the board's views or its policy for seeing that we get further television coverage in Canada in those areas that do not have it at the present time.
I do not know to whom the hon. member refers when he mentions "Indian chiefs". He mentioned something about doing away with Indian chiefs.

I did not mean that in any nasty sense. In the details listed on page 127 there are at least seven or eight people whom

I assume are senior in the organization. Then, there are a number of stenographers, and I am trying to find in there the people who are going to be doing this checking on logs and on programs to be sure that the job is done adequately.

Part of the work of examining logs is being done by the Department of Transport in co-operation with the board. Two of those listed as clerks are also checking logs. There are four others doing it as well.
That makes a total of how many people that are employed?
Six with the board and some from the Department of Transport.
Are there any plans to expand that staff or will that be the staff in that particular field?

This will depend on experience. After all, as I have said, this board is really just getting under way in its administrative work. It started just about a year ago last January and it has been conducting public hearings, formulating rules and regulations, so it really has not settled down to exercise the regular, administrative control which is part of its function. It has not had too much experience in this field because of other pressures. A year from now I think the board will be able to say exactly how many people will be required to do this work. At the moment, as I have said, they have six working on it but it may require more.

I thank the minister for that answer. Has the board ever made a statement on its position with regard to the question of further television coverage in those parts of Canada that do not have it? If they have, could they just give me the reference? If they have not, do they contemplate doing so?

The board, of course, has no authority to extend television services in any way. It has no money with which to do so. Any extension has to come either from private sources or from the C.B.C. The board certainly looks very favourably on any application, particularly one which would extend the services in what we call the rural areas, I may say the board is working with the Department of Transport in trying to simplify the rules and restrictions which heretofore have been employed in connection with those relatively small stations, attempting to make it easier to get applications through. They have spent a good deal of time on that. They have issued no paper with respect to it because, of course, it is something they have to deal with when somebody makes an application. They cannot initiate it.

The reason I raise it is, as the minister knows, that during the time we have been debating this subject the most recurrent topic has been the question of extending television coverage. I should like to get in my mind what the minister feels about this. Is the board of broadcast governors one of the places to apply pressure? I am thinking of citizens groups in my own constituency. Should they chase the board of broadcast governors in this regard or where should they go to apply pressure?

I think the first place they should go is to the bank. When they get bank credit whereby they can finance a station then they go to the Department of Transport. There is certainly no point in going to the board of broadcast governors. They deal with the applications that come before them and lay down the regulations governing them. They have no initial authority with respect to that in any way, shape or form. It has to come from private sources or the C.B.C.

I am talking about pressure groups. All of us are aware, as members of parliament, that there are community organizations that feel the government or some government agency should be working on this. I just wanted to check as to whether or not the board of broadcast governors was a pressure point for this sort of thing. I take it that it is not. The answer is one that still leaves many of us interested in this matter up in the air.
There is one other question I should like to ask the board of broadcast governors, and that is about its plans for a permanent headquarters. Have they given any consideration to that, and where do they plan to establish it? Is it going to be in Ottawa?

Ask the Minister of Public Works when his estimates are before you. The hon. member knows that the board of broadcast governors is not a separate corporation. It has not any money; it is obliged to get it from parliament. Any accommodation which is provided for it will be provided through the Department of Public Works.
I asked the minister whether he would tell the committee what had already been decided with respect to a private network.

Did the hon. member see the press release that went out? Perhaps he did not see it. I took it for granted that everyone had seen it. It is a long document. I do not want to read it all. However, there will be public hearings on September 1 and 2. What I mean is this. Discussions have been going on with the private broadcasters and with the
Supply-C.B.C.
C.B.C. Indirectly they have been kept advised. The executive members of the C.A.B. have been here. On September 1 and 2 the board is to hear oral representations on the briefs and the recommendations set out in the briefs. That is the matter to which the Globe and Mail was referring. They are having this preliminary meeting on September 1 and 2 to hear representations from public and the C.B.C. criticising or approving or whatever it may be. After that hearing and when representations and briefs are in the board will proceed to draw further regulations on a definitive basis for the setting up of this network, if it decides so to do.
I wonder if the minister can say this. It may all be in this document. However, I have only so many hours in which to read.
So have I. That is why I have not read it carefully.
The minister and I are probably in a similar situation with respect to this matter. Perhaps if I talk for a minute or two it would give him a chance to read a few lines.
I will pass it over to the hon. member and he can read it on Sunday.

I think it would be useful to have one or two points about this matter on the record. I take it, of course, that the board has no thought that the only people who will be heard at this hearing are the private television stations but that any citizen or group of citizens interested in this problem will be afforded every opportunity to be heard.
Very definitely. Steps are being taken to that end.

I am very much concerned about this matter and I am sure the minister is also concerned about it. Perhaps I should say briefly that I think it is a very sensible thing to have a private network if we are going to have this competitive group of stations. I know all the objections there were in the old days of radio to a private network and that it was prohibited for many years. But after all, as the newspaper points out tonight, we are supposed to have 17,814,000 people in this country. I think that is an increase of two thirds over what there were when the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was established in 1936. Once we are going to have these stations, I cannot imagine that it would be possible for them to sustain themselves at all without some kind of network. We know something about the cost of producing television shows.

Supply-C.B.C.
I think it is quite sensible but I think there are two considerations of which account should be taken. Perhaps because I am a penny-pincher and always have been all my life, the first thing I think about is the treasury, that is to say the taxpayers. I am somewhat concerned that we should make quite sure that we protect adequately not only the actual revenues but the potential revenues of the C.B.C. from advertising so that we are not going to take too much directly out of the treasury. I am sure the minister also is concerned.
The other thing about which I am also very much concerned is that we should not do what I said earlier about this Granada business and I am not much reassured by what the minister said on this matter a little while ago. I am very much concerned lest private television should become a kind of television Reader's Digest, if the minister understands what I mean; in other words, that stuff on which the main earnings have been made in another country will be brought out here cheaply and more or less dumped and used to attract advertising which would otherwise go into things produced in Canada by Canadians for Canadians. I should like some reassurance that these matters are really seriously in the minds of the board in connection with these hearings.

I can assure the hon. member that all these points are seriously in the minds of the board or at least of the three permanent members of the board. As the hon. member knows, there are now only two for the moment; one resigned yesterday.
Applications for the establishment of a private television network must be received by the board not later than August 1 in order to file an appearance and to be there at the meetings on September 1 and 2. That was the original plan and then it was modified to give them more time. I am told that the press release has been handed out. The hon. member, if he has time on Sunday to read it, can get there all the details dealing with it. There will be a full opportunity for representations from organizations across Canada in order to make known their views with respect to this matter. It will only be after the most careful investigation and study that the board will finally promulgate, shall we say, these ground rules and regulations.
I have no doubt in my own mind-and of this I am assured by the chairman of the board-that adequate steps will be taken to see that the Canadian content of the films or whatever there may be will be maintained at a very high standard. I do not think we need to worry at all about this becoming a sort of grandiose Reader's Digest of films
fMr. Pickersgill.]
which have made earnings perhaps in some other countries and which just come in here to be sold rather cheaply to the Canadian public. I should like to say a brief word on this item. The amount involved, on the face of it, would appear to be relatively small as far as the Department of Transport is concerned. However, this item of $8,600 represents assistance to retired railway employees, and whether or not the committee appreciates it there are in Canada several thousand retired railway workers all of whom feel that they were at one time employees of the government of Canada. This comes about because of the fact that the railways in the maritime provinces, prior to 1922 when the C.N.R. came into existence, were government-owned railways under the complete jurisdiction of the then minister of railways.
I have had a great deal of correspondence with regard to item 431 since my election to this house. I have a lot of statistics on this fund, which is administered by the Canadian National Railways, and if my information is correct the cheques which go to the several thousand former employees are issued and distributed by the Department of Transport.
For example in 1958 the fund had a total payment to pensioners in the amount of $5.9 million. That amount came from three different sources. In the first place continuing

employees put in about $145,000. The C.N.R. under the act of 1922 had to put up $100,000 annually and did so last year and the years before. The government in 1958 under this same vote put up $9,400. This year it puts up less, $8,600. The balance of the pay-out, which amounted to nearly $5.75 million, was paid for out of the general revenue of the C.N.R. In my opinion the C.N.R. has done more than its share. I do not feel the government has done its part although I do not mean to criticize the present minister nor his recent predecessor in saying that. The mistake was made in 1922.
The amount voted in recent years has been going down at a rate of about $1,000 a year. As long as there are former employees of the Intercolonial railway it will remain in the estimates and be reduced to a nil figure perhaps in the next 20 years. The 6,000 people concerned reside not only in the maritimes but in the western provinces and indeed throughout Canada. I feel that they have not been fairly treated by the federal government.
The act was set up in 1913. The employees at that time were defined as employees of Her Majesty's railway. Many of those who stayed on after 1922 when the C.N.R. took over were not eligible to join the C.N.R. pension fund in most cases because of their age. Consequently they continued to contribute 1J per cent of their wages and ended up with small pensions. I have urged the Minister of Transport, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance since 1958 to consider these several thousand people as former employees of the government of Canada. The Minister of Finance brought in legislation on July 28, 1958 and granted increases to retired members of the armed forces and the R.C.M.P. and increased the pensions of retired civil servants. At that time I had hoped that these former employees of the government of Canada, these railway employees in the maritimes, would have been considered in the same category. However, they were not included.
When the legislation became permanent in 1959, once again they were neglected. I hope that when the estimates are prepared next year this small item will completely disappear and that a new and adequate and proper amount will be included for these retired citizens.

I should like to take a few minutes to express my concern about the effects which the policy of the present government is having upon Trans-Canada Air Lines and the private transport companies. The minister has always been a very strong supporter of competition, both when he was on this side of the house and since he has moved to the treasury benches. Competition can be, and very often is, a very good thing. However, like many other good things it can be overdone and it loses its virtue when it becomes excessive. We can have too much of a good thing. In the field of transportation, excessive competition can do more harm than good. Then again, unequal competition is detestable in every field. It is very unfair when the small man has to compete with a giant, when small companies have to compete with large corporations. Under those conditions the little fellow has very little chance to survive.
The policy of the present government contrasts sharply with that of the former administration, so I propose to put it on the record so that the public can make the comparison which my hon. friends seem to desire and judge for themselves. The policy of the Liberal government was outlined by the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King on April 2, 1943 in a ministerial statement which

can be found on page 1776 of Hansard of
that date. The then prime minister began his statement as follows:
I should like to make a statement of the policy of the government on civil air transport. First with respect to domestic aviation:
Then, he went on to outline nine points of the policy which he summarized on page 1778 under the heading "Conclusion".
The policy of the Canadian government on air transport may be summed up as follows:
(a)	the government sees no good reason for changing its policy that Trans-Canada Air Lines is the sole Canadian agency which may operate international air services.
(b)	within Canada, Trans-Canada Air Lines will continue to operate all transcontinental systems, and such other services of a mainline character as may from time to time be designated by the government. Competition between air services over the same route will not be permitted whether between a publicly owned service and a privately owned service or between two privately owned services. There will remain a large field for the development of air transport in which private Canadian companies may participate, and, while preventing duplication of services, the government will continue to encourage private companies to develop services as traffic possibilities may indicate.
In the following year the Right Hon. C. D. Howe, on March 17, referred to this statement made by the prime minister on April 2, 1943, which I have just read, and elaborated that policy in these words found at page 1573 of Hansard for that date:
This statement of policy, I regret to say, failed to bring about confirmation to government policy in the development of privately owned air services within Canada, nor did it end intervention of private interests in the international field. It is becoming obvious that ownership of airways by our two competing railway systems implies extension or railway competition into transport by air. regardless of the government's desire to avoid competition between air services. In the old days, competitive railway building developed pressure methods	for	obtaining	new	franchises.	Suchmethods must not have a place in the development of	our	airways.The government desires	the	rapid developmentof air transport services in order, among other reasons, to offer post-war employment to Royal Canadian	Air	Force personnel.	Canada's	northland was pioneered by small operators who were content to enlarge their operations only as warranted by the development of the area they served. The government believes that feeder line operations, and pioneer lines into our northland, can best be developed as small operations. Our returning airmen will not be satisfied, in entering this new field of employment, to serve only as salaried employees. In this new medium of transportation, there must be a place reserved for small business enterprise.
Accordingly, after full consideration, the government has decided that the railways shall not exercise any monopoly of air services. Steps will be taken to require our railways to divest themselves of ownership of air lines, to the end that, within a period of one year from the ending of the European war, transport by air will be entirely separate from surface transportation. In the meantime, no new air routes other than government operated routes will be allocated to airlines owned

by any railway or other operator of surface transportation. The term "surface transportation" Includes railways, shipping companies, and highway transport companies.
That policy was designed specifically to protect the small, independent operator. In order to obtain a correct picture, it is necessary to go back to the days of the early development of civil aviation in Canada. When the former Liberal government decided to develop civil aviation in Canada, they were anxious to avoid having the competition between the two railway systems extended into the field of air transportation. Therefore, when they decided to set up Trans-Canada Air Lines in 1937, they envisaged a partnership between private enterprise and public enterprise, with private enterprise owning the air lines and the government providing airports, terminals and communications.
Accordingly, then, the Canadian Pacific railway, Canadian National Railways and Canadian Airways Limited were invited to provide the capital and to share equally in the ownership of Trans-Canada Air Lines. This corporation was to have a nine-man board of directors on which each of the companies would have two representatives. By reason of its capital investment in airports and terminals, the government would have three directors. The C.P.R. and the Canadian Airways withdrew then because they objected to the government having any directors on the board. This action left the Canadian National Railways as the sole owner.
In order to protect the small bush operators and to prevent cutthroat competition there was passed in 1938 an amendment to the Railway Act to allocate routes to the companies that were then in the field and to prevent competition in those routes through newly formed companies. Shortly after that time world war II broke out and along with that came a sharp curtailment in the gold mining operations which created most of the traffic for the independent operators. This curtailment of their business forced them in time either to find new buyers or to close down their operations. At this stage the Canadian Pacific railway entered the field of air transportation and bought up all the stock of the independent operators so that by 1941 Canadian Pacific Air Lines had obtained a monopoly in the air transportation field except for Trans-Canada Air Lines. A full account of this is given in Hansard of March 17, 1944 at pages 1571-72.
Then came the construction of the Alaska highway and it was fortunate for the Canadian airlines that this development took place in the territory which C.P.A. served. It was fortunate also that the United States

had a strong military interest in this project. That interest was such that the C.P.A. were able to get new and modern equipment from United States sources at a time when all other companies found it impossible to get new equipment.
Recent press reports of the effects of government policy on independent operators and activities of Bristol Aeroplane Company of Canada in buying up Spartan Air Lines Limited and negotiating for the purchase of other air lines would indicate that history is about to repeat itself. I would therefore ask the minister to take another look at his policy and to see whether competition has not been going perhaps a little too far.

In answer to that question I would simply say that the hon. member has compared today's events and operations with those of 1943. I would remind him that that is 17 years ago. In 1943 the revenues of all airlines were somewhere between $20 million and $25 million a year. Today T.C.A. revenues alone are over $100 million and the total revenue of all airlines is $225 million, or an increase of ten times over that former period. A great many changes have developed in the air industry since that time. Our policy of modified competition is, we believe, more in keeping with today's air needs and is designed to supply better and more service to the travelling and shipping public. We believe that is the obligation of the government in a matter of this kind. We believe that our policy is the one that is most suited to today's needs.

the Wheatcroft report, which is that of a British expert and an excellent report it is. Following that report no statement of policy was made by the minister either in the one field or the other.
He has said here tonight that there is some question of competition. But in a field as important as is that of air service surely there should be a clear-cut policy either in agreement with what was done by the former administration or in contradiction to it because of changed circumstances.
