It seems to me that is a matter to which the minister must give consideration in conjunction with the officers of his department. He may do it between sessions. He may do it before the end of the session. However, I think there must be an explanation of why we are having the operations and the actions which are taking place in the international field as well as in the domestic field.
I spoke in Timmins in February, 1958 and I gave what I considered to be a reasoned and full statement of this government's policy with regard to air operations.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Will the minister allow me a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Does the minister not think that a matter of this kind should be announced in the house.

To be quite honest, I may say that things were happening quite fast at that time. In all truthfulness I may say I had intended to make this statement in the house. I think the date on which I made it was February 8, 1958. As the hon. member will recall, the house was dissolved quite suddenly and quite unexpectedly on February 1, I believe, exactly seven days previously. I had the statement all ready. Naturally I was prepared to give it in the house and of course I would have done so but events caught up with me and I had a statement but no house to which to give it. Therefore, knowing that the hon. member and the air industry would want a statement as soon as possible, I made it as quickly as I could. I chose an opportunity when I had been asked to speak at a banquet in Timmins and gave the air statement at that time.

Supply-Transport

I should like to speak rather briefly on the question of regional airports. For a good many years I have been associated with the development of a regional airport and I fully appreciate the problems confronting municipalities in areas of that kind in connection with the provision of air services. Basically, the duty of a municipality is to look after the people in matters of education, health, welfare and things of that nature. The provision of large sums of money in order to put in the facilities for a regional airport is something that is beyond the ability of the municipality. I realize that there are certain benefits that come to an airport where they can provide a scheduled air passenger service; but in a community in which there is a density of population and also an accumulation of industry there is definitely a need for a regional airport in order to provide the facilities for non-scheduled flights for both industrial and passenger service.
I cannot help but refer to the riding I represent. In that riding we have quite a considerable amount of industry and many of those industries have executive aircraft. We have the facilities to keep them but we do not have suitable runways, which means that some of them are kept at Buffalo, New York, some at Niagara Falls, New York, some at Malton and some at Mount Hope. This is a situation we would like to correct, but unfortunately are not in a position to extend the runways.
I might also say that in my riding we have at least one industry and rather than build a great concentration of manufacturing in our area, plants have been built in Winnipeg, Regina and also in Calgary. They have planes which are flying back and forth all the time and we certainly need a place to keep them at our regional airport.
Another problem we have is that we have several plants there connected with auto parts. One of those plants has built warehouses at practically all the large airports across Canada so that they can fly the parts in in a hurry so they will be there when required.
That also brings me to the point that we need more services in our locality. I do not like to take up time talking about my own riding but I am sure that the conditions which prevail in Lincoln county are much the same as in many other ridings. If you happen to be located on a route where you have a T.C.A. airport close by, the problem is not so great, but if you are in an area which is too close to a large airport or too far away, then you have the problem of providing service.
I am just bringing these matters to the attention of the minister and I hope he will give them serious consideration. I have been
[Mr. Hees.l
very much pleased in the past by some of the speeches the minister has made when he has referred to the great possibilities of packaged freight being picked up and delivered by airplane, and that is just along my thinking. I feel that we have to march with the times and there is no doubt that the airplane is a popular way to travel today and is becoming more and more so as time goes on. As I say, any municipality which has a concentration of industry and a density of population has a definite need for a regional airport, which is a matter beyond the ability of most municipalities to provide.

Mr. Chairman, on June 23 last I asked the minister the following question, as reported on page 5287 of Hansard:
Could the minister say what steps are being taken to avert tragedies similar to that which recently occurred on lake Williams, Nova Scotia, when a boy was drowned because a pilot, taking off from the lake, failed to notice the sailboat in which he was a passenger?
The minister replied as follows:
Under the air regulations certain regulatory procedures aimed at guarding against mishaps of this nature are prescribed. We have not yet received from our district officials the formal report with respect to the tragedy referred to by the hon. member.
This accident was brought to the attention of the Department of Transport at Moncton, and on June 28, at 7.40 p.m., a seaplane bearing the affix "KSF" proceeded immediately from Halifax flying club down the extreme western end of lake Williams at an excessive speed and an accident would have happened if a swimmer had been in the water there or a boat had been backing out from the jetty. When it is realized that in the last fatal accident the pilot did not kill his motor and the propellor was in motion the feeling of the residents may better be appreciated.
I should be grateful if the minister would see that an investigation is carried out with the least possible delay in view of the anxiety of the people in the lake Williams area of Nova Scotia.

I hate to be a dead horse all the time, but I have an airfield which needs a strip. The minister wrote me a nice letter and I had it published in the paper, and when I was out there last Saturday everybody came along and said "Why, you big boob, what is wrong there? Can't you get anything from that government?" So I want the minister to build this strip for me. Dawson Creek is the centre of the oil country.

I wonder if the minister would tell the house whether or not his department carried out an investigation into the causes of the death of three men in the Nahanni

valley recently when an aircraft was to pick up a party some time in March but did not make the pick-up? As a result three men starved to death and two were fortunately saved sometime in May.
Mr. Chairman, I have not seen the report from our investigation branch but I assure the hon. member I will ask for it and look into the matter right away.

A supplementary question.
When the minister has the report I wonder if he would consider some sort of regulation whereby air operators, particularly those working in northern Canada in isolated areas, who accept charters to take men to the bush and have pick-up dates to return these men from the bush, in cases of break-up or freeze-up are required to notify the local R.C.M.P. detachment so that someone in the area at least knows there are people in the bush and can pick them up?
That would be an air transport board regulation rather than a Department of Transport regulation, but I would be very glad to recommend this to the chairman of the air transport board.

Mr. Chairman, I have only a couple of questions and I trust the minister will answer when he replies to the various matters which have been brought to his attention under this first item of the air services division. Will he inform the committee who were the directors of Trans-Canada Air Lines on January 1 of this year and whether there has been any resignations and appointments since and, if so, who they are?

I have not the list here because
the hon. member knows that the estimates of Trans-Canada Air Lines came up earlier in the year. Therefore I do not have that information available. I can tell the hon. member, however, that there was one resignation and one new appointment, the resignation of Mr. Frank Ross of Vancouver and the appointment in his place of Mr. Hackett of Vancouver.
One further question. Would the minister consider that it would be proper for members of parliament to criticize the work of a director of the T.C.A. in this committee on the proper item?

I would think that would be a matter which would more properly be brought up when the estimates of the T.C.A. are considered, earlier in the session, at the same time as the Canadian National Railways. I do not know of any item on these estimates which would justify such a discussion.
Supply-Transport

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to know what disposition is to be made, or has been made, of some of the small, auxiliary air stations which were built all across the country, most of them in the depression days. Most of them are now too small for modern aircraft. In the area which I represent there are five or six of these airfields which are no longer kept up. The bush is no longer cut, and weeds have been allowed to grow. It is true there are range lights on some of them, but I imagine the lighting equipment is insufficient.
I have had some correspondence with one of my constituents in connection with one of these airfields. As a matter of fact, he wants to buy part of it. I have been given to understand that the federal authorities gave it back to the province of Ontario, but the province says that is not the case and that the land is still registered in the name of the federal government. After considerable correspondence I am unable to find out how this property has been disposed of.
I should like to know whether these airfields are being returned to the provincial governments so that use may be made of them. Perhaps it is the intention of the department to retain these auxiliary fields, in which case I think some work should be done on them so that they might serve their purpose adequately. We have been receiving many complaints that weeds have been left to grow uncontrolled and so on. If these places are no longer of any value I suppose we should begin to dispose of them.

Each individual case is dealt with separately, and if there is need of an airfield it is kept in operation. Should the municipality wish to take over any particular field we are glad to allow the municipality to do so, and we are prepared to assist the municipality to develop it. We have a definite policy in this regard, and we can co-operate on a cost-sharing basis up to a contribution of $100,000. As hon. members may know, if a scheduled airline indicates its desire to make a regular call at a particular field in a given locality the government will develop that airfield on its own. Each case is dealt with on its merits, and if the hon. member or any other hon. member has a particular airfield which he would like to bring to our attention we will give it close consideration and let him know what can be done with regard to that particular field. If airfields are not likely to be needed in the future we are very glad to turn them back to the municipality, or sell them, or make the best disposal of them that we can.

Supply-Transport

In the riding of Nickel Belt we have an airstrip which needs a little attention. The minister may recall that we have had some correspondence concerning improvements which seemed to be required in order to permit civilians to use an airstrip which had been constructed by citizens or corporations in the vicinity of Gogama. Recently I had occasion to fly over that area, using a seaplane, in order to inspect the floods in Foleyet. The strip is visible from the air. Although the letter I received from the minister indicated that he was renewing an investigation into the possibility of assisting those interested in this airstrip to bring it into such a condition that it could be used by tourists from the United States, that letter is now nearly a year old. I realize that the minister may not be in a position to give an immediate and clear answer with regard to this question of providing assistance so that the airstrip might be adapted for a certain degree of commercial use. However, I feel that the investigation which he has promised should be carried out so that proper information could be furnished to the people of this great area of northern Ontario who would undoubtedly benefit if this service could be provided through an extension of the existing airstrip. At the present time the facilities are limited.
I shall be glad to look into that particular case.

Before this item carries I wonder if the minister could tell me if there are any regulations in his department restricting in any way the participation of airline pilots in activites in connection with reserve squadrons of the R.C.A.F.
Not that I am aware.

I should like to say a few words about this question of policy which was opened by the hon. member for Laurier and spoken to by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. It seems to me in so far as one can discern the policy of the government from the rather excited election speech that the minister made in Timmins on February 8, 1958, which he did not think it worth while in the two years since to repeat in the house, and from one or two answers he has given to questions, that the policy which was followed from 1944 onward by the previous administration has been abandoned for something which we have to try to formulate for ourselves because the government, which I suspect does not really know what it is doing, is unable to explain.
In so far as one can discern, it is a precise contradiction of what the Minister of Justice is trying to do in another field. In the retail

field we have this government trying to eliminate competition. At the same time we have the Minister of Transport professing to increase competition. In itself that may not necessarily be something to condemn, because there are some fields in which it is perfectly clear that competition is neither desirable nor, in fact, in any real sense, possible. We have never had a competitive post office in this country and I do not think anybody would ever argue for one. On the other hand I hope the efforts of the Minister of Justice will never get to the point where the retail outlets are limited and prices are dictated by a few manufacturers.
Misinterpretation.
It seems to me that is what this government is trying surreptitiously to do in another field.
Nonsense.

On a point of order, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is seeking to bring into this debate an item which is at present before the banking and commerce committee, and I think that is improper in these circumstances.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
On the point of order, I am sure the committee will be of the view that it is not out of order in discussing a matter under	air services	to make	acomparison	with another	matter	eventhough that	other matter	is under	discussion in	another place,	provided	the
member does not deal in toto with the matter which is under discussion by the committee. It seems to me that has been the practice in this house from time to time. All that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was doing-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We know what he was doing.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We certainly do not know what you are doing most of the time.
Sleeping.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: All that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was doing was comparing the position in this field with that in another field.

I do not suppose that you wish to rule on the point of order, Mr. Chairman, but if you do I shall be glad to take my seat. As the Prime Minister said yesterday, the bill of rights has not passed yet, but I suppose we still have freedom to make analogies in this committee-
If they are accurate.

-or even to point out the most extraordinary contrasts. That is all I was trying to do. From the expression on the

face of the Minister of Transport I suspect that he wishes to restrain the freedom of speech of some of his friends. I can understand his feeling.
I want to get back to what is, after all, a very serious matter. I am not talking about the transcontinental air service or the international service but about the local services, the kind, in so far as I have been able to discern from what has happened, that have been decontrolled by the government where-[DOT] I forget what adjective the minister used but he described it as some kind of competition- competition now prevails. This is a field which like the telephone field, the taxi field and many other fields where obviously there is in a sparsely populated country like this only a relatively limited amount of business. Buying air services is not like buying potatoes. The average person can judge a potato just as well as the Minister of Transport or the air transport board can but the average person is handicapped in judging the safety and reliability of an air service.
It is for that reason, and for that reason alone that this parliament years ago felt it necessary to set up the board of railway commissioners to regulate railways in this country. It was for the same reason that the government in 1944 felt it necessary to set up the air transport board which I believe has served this country well ever since and I think would continue to serve it well if it were allowed to do so but it has not been allowed to do so in the last couple of years.
The result has been that far from increasing competition in certain sections of the country what this is doing is enabling one or two carriers to gobble up their competitors or to put them out of business. If the present trend continues we are going to have happen exactly what was happening in western Canada just before the war and in the early years of the war. We are going to have only one or two carriers left in this whole field and they are going to be centralized in one or two places in central Canada and possibly in Vancouver, and we are not going to have any local services left. I do not believe that will be more economical for the people of Canada and certainly it will not give us better service.
Those of us who have some experience of the remoter and more sparsely settled parts of Canada know what a tremendous advantage it is to have a local airline where the pilots, the management and everybody concerned know the local conditions and where you can get the kind of service you cannot possibly get when the management is centralized thousands of miles away. It seems to me that what the government has done is a very retrograde step indeed. It is resulting
Supply-Transport
in driving a number of people out of business and in consolidating other businesses in a way that is going to prove to be wholly detrimental to the Canadian air industry. In fact it has already proven to be detrimental.
From the history of what has happened in this field in the last two years one cannot escape this suspicion. Perhaps even more one cannot escape the suspicion that this decontrolled policy will not be of long range advantage to the people of this country. Perhaps the reason it has never been enunciated in this chamber is that it is not a policy at all but merely an attempt to favour one or two particular companies such as Autair and Georgian Bay about whom my friend the hon. member for Laurier has told us a good deal already.
When the minister replies I should like him to tell us this. The minister is such a champion of the little people I should like to have him tell us what little people are the shareholders of Georgian Bay. I think it might be quite illuminating to the committee if we could have an explanation. What is clearly happening is that decontrol is taking place so that one or two wealthy companies can gobble up the rest. If this continues we will cease to have the network of local services which has served this country so well, advanced transportation in the remote areas so much and been such a benefit to the people over the last 15 years.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member laid quite a stress on what he claimed was the gobbling up of the air services so that there would be only one or two air services left in the country, I believe he said.
I said that would be the end result.

That is what I said you said. Perhaps the hon. member was not present in the early part of the discussion when in answer to a question asked, I believe by the hon. member for Laurier, I said that the net increase-and again I stress the net increase -of licences issued during the past 22 months was 118 new licences.
To commercial operators?

Yes. These provide new services and much more adequate services to the travelling and shipping public. This, Mr. Chairman, I claim is no diminution of services in Canada. It is a tremendous increase in services to the travelling and shipping public, something which never could have occurred under the policy of the government of which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was a member.

Supply-Transport
The hon. member also said that there would be some detrimental effect on safety standards as a result of this new policy.
I did not say that at all.
Then I apologize, Mr. Chairman. I understood that is what the hon. member inferred.
No, I did not.
I wish to assure the hon. member that there is no diminution in safety standards. Our safety standards are for all aircraft flying.
I hope they are.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I said that with reference to Autair and the minister has never replied to that statement.

At the request of the hon. member for Laurier I looked up the accident record for Autair and as I indicated to him privately the accident record of Autair is neither at the top nor at the bottom of the scale but just about the middle-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is pretty bad.
-of the accident record of all companies operating in Canada.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is pretty bad.

If the hon. member for Laurier says that the accident record for Autair is pretty bad then he obviously thinks that the average performance of all aircraft companies in Canada is pretty bad, or certainly the average company in Canada.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I said that the operations of Autair were pretty bad.
I said that the operations of Autair were just about average so therefore the hon. member is saying that the operations of the average aircraft carrier in Canada are pretty bad.

Or else the minister's
arithmetic is pretty bad.

No, the minister's arithmetic is not bad in this particular case.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate drew attention to what he claimed was a difference of opinion between myself and the Minister of Justice in legislation which the minister is introducing. I would say there is no substance in that. This government believes in reasonable, sensible competition and I believe that all hon. members would agree that that is a good objective. That is what we are after in all fields of endeavour and that,
I think, would find commendation among the general public.

I should like to put a specific question to the minister. I am afraid

I do not know this terminology very well. Not counting C.P.A. or T.C.A. would the minister say how many companies there were engaged in operations in 1957 and how many aircraft they had, and how many companies there are in operation today and how many aircraft they have in the commercial field?
Order paper.

Mr. Chairman, there is certainly an increase but the hon. member would not expect me to have those particular figures at my fingertips. I assure him I will get them as soon as possible and see that he receives them.

The minister is quite wrong when he says that I would not expect him to have them. I would not come into committee to put through my estimates without having such information. When the previous government was in office and my hon. friend from Laurier was where the minister is he did have such information and he supplied a lot of iti. as I recall very well.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am somewhat surprised by the statement which the minister made. I have made certain charges in the house with reference to Autair and I have no recollection of the minister ever replying to them save and except what he said tonight. The question that comes to my mind now is, what is the present position of Autair? I asked the minister on the orders of the day repeatedly whether they had sold their interests; whether they have been taken over by Bristol Air Services and the only reply I got from the minister was, "Well, oh, the hon. member for Laurier knows the answer to that question", and he sat down. The minister has the habit of answering questions in that way and he gets away with it on the orders of the day but he cannot do that nearly as easily on his estimates. The minister should tell us what is the position of that air company which had seven accidents in 1959 and six in 1960, and which did not reply to the air transport board in so far as proving financial responsibility is concerned, which refused peremptorily to reply to a letter from the air transport board asking it to file financial responsibility with the board, which disregarded the instructions of the board and for that reason the board turned down its application.
Does the minister still think that this is the kind of air service or aircraft company that should be operating in this country and getting very large contracts from the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys? Not only was its insurance cancelled but it had difficulty getting insurance from other companies. My

information is that the air transport board is not satisfied to this day with the financial responsibility of that company.
Will the minister tell the committee what is the position of the company; whether it has been sold; whether it is still in operation; whether it is still in good standing? Surely, we ought to be able to know what is happening in that field. Notwithstanding the many statements I have made in this house, this is the only time, unless my memory fails me, that the minister has made any attempt to reply to these charges.

Perhaps the hon. member does not recall but I recall it very well. We walked out of the chamber together and between that door and the elevator we discussed this matter. As I remember it, I told him what the particular safety standards required of Autair had been, and he appeared quite interested at the time. Perhaps he was busy and no doubt he has forgotten about it. I assure him the conversation did take place. I am sure he did not think that I had told him because otherwise I would have written him a letter. I think he will agree that when he asks questions I do give him an answer.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I interrupt the minister to say that he is quite right; he did speak to me privately as we went out of the chamber but the point is that these charges have been put on the record. Although the minister did give me an explanation which, in my opinion, was not satisfactory, I think the explanation, if there is one, should be put on the record. The explanation which the minister has given tonight, in my opinion, is not satisfactory. I think he should reply to the questions I have asked him.

The hon. member feels that the answer I have given him is not satisfactory; I feel it is. An investigation was made into the safety record of Autair, as I have told him tonight, and we were satisfied with the report we got regarding the safety standards of Autair. They were not at the top of the list, nor were they at the bottom of the list; they were somewhere around average.
With regard to the present position of Autair, an application has been made to buy out Autair by another aircraft company and that application is before the board at the present time for approval.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I understand that that application has been before the board now for at least two months. Can the minister say why it is not being disposed of?

My information is it is only recently that the application has been received by the board.
Supply-Transport

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I asked the minister that question on the orders of the day at least one month ago, if not longer.
I am advised that the offer was made about two months ago, but I am also advised that it was not submitted to the board for approval until recently.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: After the air transport board heard the application of Autair to be relieved of certain restrictions it declined the application. Can the minister tell the committee the reasons why the application was declined by the air transport board?

This happened some time ago when the board was bound by the regulations set up for it by the previous government. On looking into cases of this kind I came to the conclusion that these restrictions were too rigid and that the aircraft industry generally and the travelling and shipping public would benefit if those restrictions were made less rigid and that a general easing up of this policy should take place, and that was done. I believe that results have been good.
As I have said, during the 22 months since that time a net increase of 118 new commercial licences have been issued, and this is supplying greatly improved and increased service to the shipping and travelling public. I think that is the kind of thing that the government should do for the taxpayers of the country which it serves.

The minister has twice used the figure of 118 additional licences. Of course, that by itself means absolutely nothing. What would mean something is to know how many aircraft it represents and what increase there has been in the number of aircraft, the classes of aircraft and so on. Just to give a figure like that pulled out of the air means nothing whatsoever. Because the minister tossed that figure out as a kind of airy reply to a serious question that I put, I asked him how many companies were operating in 1957 and how many there are today; how many aircraft did they have and what is their carrying capacity, and these other things, so that a valid comparison could be made.
I have a view as to what is happening as a result of the minister's policy, but I do not pretend to be an expert in this field; I am merely a representative of some of the taxpayers seeking information.

I think the hon. member will readily appreciate the fact that this discussion should properly take place on item 451, which deals with matters that come under the air transport board, and when the chairman of the air transport board is at the table I shall be able to give him those figures.

Supply-Transport
Neither of the gentlemen at this table has them in his head and certainly I have not either.
I shall be quite happy to defer the discussion until that time. Would the minister prefer to wait until then to answer the question I put to him about Georgian Bay?
Yes, I shall be very glad to give the hon. member the information.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister how many planes there are in the Department of Transport. I understood some time ago that since the minister took over there has been one new Viscount purchased. Then later on I think there was an additional one purchased, unless I am mistaken. Now I am informed that the fleet has been augmented by the purchase of a 550-mile an hour Lockheed Jetstar plane to carry eight passengers and a crew of two and that delivery of the new aircraft is scheduled for next year. Is that correct?
Yes, that is correct.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Will the minister tell the house what the cost of the new plane will be, and how many planes there are in the Department of Transport?
The cost of the new plane will be approximately $1 million. We have 15 helicopters and 35 aircraft, most of which are in regional stations.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: How many are in Ottawa?

We have that information here. There are two Viscounts; four DC-3's; four Beechcraft; one PA-23; one Beaver and 11 helicopters. The Beechcraft and the DC-3's are aircraft reserved for use in the various districts.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The only point I desire to make in connection with that is that on an earlier occasion when we were discussing vote 419 a great deal was made of the fact that one of the railway cars had been taken off and a substantial saving of money had been obtained-
I do not believe I said a substantial saving of money had been obtained. I just mentioned that we had taken off one car and were considering taking off another car.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am saying that a substantial saving of money must, of necessity, follow the cancellation of the operation of a railway car. However, what that amounts to is infinitesimal in comparison to the cost of the additional Viscount that has been purchased, and still more infinitesimal in comparison

with the new Lockheed Jetstar plane to carry eight passengers and a crew of two.
The question, of course, that arises is that taxpayers have a reason to wonder why, with the services of Canadian Pacific Air Lines and Trans-Canada Air Lines available, the Department of Transport finds it necessary to provide additional air transport at considerable public expense. There are today facilities in Canada, both through Trans-Canada Air Lines and Canadian Pacific Air Lines, to handle any amount of government air travel that may be required and duplication of the services of regular carriers by a department of government sometimes lacks sense.
I would not have raised the question had there not been such stress laid upon the fact that one of the railway cars was being cancelled. As opposed to that here is not only tremendous capital sums of money being spent but the operational costs of an aircraft in comparison to those of a railway car, are great. I know, and I do not in the slightest degree complain, about the necessity of a minister of transport being able to move around fast in this country. No one, certainly not myself, will ever raise that question. But surely one Viscount, which is a fast plane, with several additional planes, a Beechcraft, a Lodestar and a DC-4, I believe-
No, a DC-3.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: A DC-3, not a DC-4; the minister corrects me. There are plenty of aircraft to allow the minister to fulfil his responsibilities, which are important, all of us know, in the light of modem transport problems. I bring this to the attention of the commitee, and compare it with the saving accomplished by the reduction of one railway car.

The DC-3's and Beechcraft are used almost entirely for calibration purposes. The additional Viscounts which were added to the Viscount which the government of which he was a member previously purchased were purchased for departmental use, and perhaps the committee would be interested in hearing something about this matter.
The department in addition to its fleet of helicopters for marine use and conventional reciprocal engine aircraft, ranging from single-engine Beavers to twin-engine DC-3's, operates two turbine-propeller Viscount aircraft and has recently placed an order for a Lockheed Jetstar, a small ten-passenger pure jet type civil aircraft.
The reasons for acquiring turbine-powered aircraft were explained by the parliamentary assistant to my predecessor in office on April 6, 1955, in a statement he made to this house. The highlight of this statement, to my mind,

was his emphasis on the fact that the Department of Transport is responsible for setting and enforcing standards for flying in Canada, whether in the field of personnel licences, route operating certificates, air traffic control or other matters. In order to set adequate standards and to maintain a continual check on these, departmental personnel must be fully competent and up to date, and it is impossible to maintain competence based only upon the use of the older type piston engine aircraft. The flight experience that we are gaining from the turbine engine aircraft, which we actually own and operate ourselves, is worth far more to the department and to the standards of aviation safety as a whole than the price we have paid for this aircraft.
To give an example, quite apart from better experience and better training of personnel, in future the flight checks on ground aids to navigation, such as radio guiding devices, must be performed at a much higher altitude than hitherto, and this work cannot be done by the older type piston engine aircraft.
While it is the case that upon occasion this plane may be used to provide special transportation for ministers of the crown or foreign heads of state in a fashion that is entirely appropriate to the twentieth century, the primary requirement of my department is in accordance with the reasons that I have given in this statement. I might add that wherever commercial air lines are available, government personnel travel by these commercial air lines.

I should like to ask the minister if his department is giving some consideration to the improvement of the facilities at the airport at the lakehead, Fort William airport. I have received complaints from a number of people concerning the inadequacy of the departmental facilities at this airport. I asked our airport manager if he had any instructions to enlarge the departmental facilities at the airport and he replied he had no such instructions and he was not authorized to enlarge the accommodations because such instructions had to come from Ottawa.
I merely wish to point out to the minister that the need is apparent to anyone who visits the airport at Fort William. I should like also to ask the minister if the department contemplates the extension of the facilities at the airport, such as the terminal building. It is only seven years old, but it is already too small to handle the traffic which is increasing at a great rate, just as it is at most airports in Canada. Will the minister give a report on that?
Supply-Transport
As to the lakehead airport, may I say that we have in the planning stage an expansion of the lakehead air terminal.
Following up the answer given by the minister, may I ask what is the expansion? What would it mean? What is the contemplated expansion? Will it be an administration building?
It includes an administration building and facilities for departmental personnel.
Is that for the near future? Is it for the immediate future?
Yes. Plans are not ready at the present time but it is authorized for a start later in this fiscal year and we hope to be able to make that start.

I just want to reinforce the interest of the hon. member for Fort William in this particular matter and to mention particularly that regional chambers of commerce and labour councils have been interested in it. I did not hear the hon. member for Fort William say it specifically, but it is a means of providing winter employment. I just remind the minister, in case he does not know, that we have one of the highest unemployment situations in Canada. If plans could be pushed to have airport construction going next winter it would perhaps be a small but important measure in helping to relieve the situation and I hope he will keep that matter in mind.

We will do everything possible to get this program going so that it may provide winter employment. I am well aware of the situation at the lakehead with regard to employment which the hon. member has just mentioned.

I just want to say a few words here. In Regina, because of the foresight of the present administration, expansion plans were adopted and they have been going ahead very well. The question raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur with regard to a building seven years old being too small rather indicates the lack of foresight of the previous administration. In Regina the question raised by the hon. member for Fort William was taken into consideration. Our expansion program was started. It went on through the winter and provided jobs for winter employment. We hope it will be finished soon and that there will be an opening of these facilities later this year. On behalf of my constituency may I say that we appreciate the attention and foresight of the department and the minister and we look forward to having our new facilities very shortly.

Supply-Transport
Before the vote carries, will the minister give us the latest target date for the completion of the Winnipeg airport?
It has not changed. Once we set a target date we stick to it.
Will the minister say what it is so that it will be on the record?
Yes; I said previously, and I say it again, that we will have it ready by 1964 at the latest and we hope to have it ready considerably before that time.
What about Dorval?
I am very glad to advise the hon. member that it is ahead of schedule.
Which schedule?
The only schedule; the schedule that will complete it this year.

The schedules and deadlines the minister is talking about must be something like the schedules of many of the unscheduled air lines out on the coast of British Columbia-they are subject to change without notice. I want to say that we have not been so fortunate in Prince Rupert as has the hon. member for Regina. I wonder whether the minister could perhaps outline to the committee, even though he has done this by correspondence with myself, for the benefit of city council and interested parties in Prince Rupert, just what is taking place with respect to the airport at Prince Rupert. What are the schedules or deadlines for completion of the various projects there and when will the airport be fully completed?
We are now proceeding with plans for that air terminal. We will get them going just as soon as we can. We hope to get them going later in this fiscal year.
Will the minister indicate what the deadline or schedule for completion is?
It will take, we expect, about a year after the start is made.
There is no definite deadline or schedule as there is in the case of Dorval and Winnipeg?
No. We do not make any deadline until we are sure of it.
Can the minister say whether architectural plans for the Winnipeg air terminal are completed yet?
Yes. The first three contracts have been let for that air terminal. We expect to call tenders for the final contract in August or September.
That was not a direct answer to my question but from it may I draw the inference that all of the architectural plans are complete in every detail?
They will be complete by the time we call the final tender.
Then the architectural plans the minister said were completed last year were just some pencil sketches on a piece of paper; is that correct?
No. Those were not plans for the finishing. They were layout plans.
Those were for the foundation?
No. They were layout plans.
I wonder whether the minister could say what the schedule is for the new Toronto air terminal and when he expects it to be completed?
Roughly, the same as for the Winnipeg air terminal. We will finish it by 1964, we expect, and sooner if possible.
Did I understand the minister to say that he was calling at least three different contracts for the terminal in Winnipeg?
Yes. There are separate contracts for the foundation work, the steel work and general finishing.

Has the minister consulted with the senior builder of the government, the crown prince from Rosedale, who told us in the public accounts committee a couple of years ago that the greatest mistake a government could make was to let several contracts for the same building, that the plans should all be completed first before any contract was called and a firm estimate should be obtained in advance as to what it would cost? Will the minister consult with the hon. member for Rosedale and ascertain whether the government can reach a concerted policy in this matter?

As the hon. member will be interested to hear, the building of an air terminal building is quite different from the building of an ordinary public works building. There are a great many technical features, as the hon. member for Laurier well knows, that must be incorporated in an air terminal building and the construction program is one that has different requirements from those of a straight public works building. In calling for the tenders for which we are calling, we believe this is the best and the most efficient way of getting the job done in the quickest and most efficient manner.
It is too complicated for the Minister of Public Works.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I know the minister will be pleased to hear me say that I agree with what he has just said in connection with airport terminal buildings. That was the position so far as Dorval was concerned; it was the position so far as Uplands was concerned and it was the position in so far as many other airports were concerned. But the point my friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was making was that the hon. member for Rosedale, now the Minister of Public Works, pooh-poohed all of that, and said there was no substance to it, when we made this statement in the committee on public accounts.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: We all enjoyed it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
He made it quite clear that any of us who maintained that was the position which should be taken should have his head examined. He maintained that the construction industry made it quite clear that the planning should be completed before the terminal building should be initiated.
Then there is another thing which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister and which was often brought to my attention by the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he sat on this side of the house. He felt that it was silly to have two construction departments, one in the Department of Public Works and another in the Department of Transport. He said that was duplication and that it was overlapping. "We must do away with that; it will cut costs," he said. I would get up and make the best possible defence I could under the circumstance, but no, the Secretary of State for External Affairs would insist. Therefore I would like either the Minister of Transport or the Minister of Public Works when his estimates are before the house to give us some indication whether or not there is any tendency in either of these two departments to do away with that duplication so that there will only be one construction branch.
But I did not rise with that in mind. I rose with something else in mind and it was the statement which just knocked me off balance which the minister made in connection with Dorval airport. He announced this and said "Once we set a target we stick to it". He set a target in connection with the Dorval airport several times but he never stuck to it. That happened on at least three occasions.
They are stuck with it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That looks very much to be the case. Does the minister remember that
Supply-Transport
on August 26, 1957 there emanated from his office a press release, part of which reads as follows.
Read it all.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No; it would take too long and I would like to assist the committee in passing these estimates to the extent I can. It reads in this way:
Tenders for the general contract for the interior of the building have been invited and these will close early in October, a transport department official stated. The contract will likely be awarded late in October.
That was 1957. Then it goes on further to say:
It is estimated that the building will near completion late in 1958 but it will take some months after that before installation of the complex operational equipment can be finished. Tentative opening date for the terminal is spring 1959.
And the cost at that time was estimated at $12 million. Then the minister on Saturday, September 7, 1957, speaking before the Canadian international air show dinner in Toronto made the following statement:
In two more years the demand for greatly increased airport facilities will be upon us. In these two years we must complete the construction of the six terminals now underway, namely Ottawa, Montreal, Gander, St. John's, Windsor and Quebec city, and start construction on six to eight new terminals.
That would mean that the construction of the Dorval airport should be terminated by
1959.
Then finally-
Not finally.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, perhaps not finally, but on November 19, 1959, in accordance with a statement appearing in the Montreal Gazette, it is stated that:
Transport minister Hees led a troupe of M.P.s and departmental officials to the partially completed terminal at Montreal airport yesterday and said the new building would be ready next year- "as I always claimed it would be."
So there you have three different statements in connection with Dorval; one in 1957, one in 1959 and one in 1960.
You will still have a good airport.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes. The airport which I have seen will be a credit, I am sure, to Canada, and I am happy to take this occasion to say that it will be one of the finest airports in our country. I have seen it on at least two occasions. The minister has not liked the fact that although I was invited I did not join the troupe of M.P.s on the occasion in question. I did not join them for a very obvious reason, because had I joined them and I had

Supply-Transport
been asked for my opinion in connection with the progress of the work, I would have criticized it bitterly. Because at the time I rose in the house, and I rose on several occasions, there was no doubt that the progress of the construction of that airport had bogged down tremendously.
I am happy to see that that position has changed substantially, and if that is so I am positive that it is due in some measure to the constructive criticism that came from this side of the house. I am also happy to be able to say that it is going to be a tremendous advancement for Montreal, but I do hope that the minister will not again say "When we make statements about target dates we stick to them", because in this case that did not happen.

Mr. Chairman, I certainly made that statement in the form of a press release on September 7, 1957, and as the hon. member realizes that is about two months after we took over. At that time I had not realized really how much this airport had bogged down under the previous administration. It really took several months before I realized what a catastrophic state the whole thing was in. After that we were able to make a proper forecast, and that forecast I have stuck to. I certainly did make the statement in September 1957, but I have no recollection of making any statement in 1959, as the hon. member said.
In 1958, at the dinner.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I recall the occasion.
In 1959 I do not -remember when I took the tour around the airport with members of parliament.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The dinner which the Minister of Transport addressed was the Canadian international air show dinner at Toronto in 1957.

Mr. Chairman, when I said that in 1957 I still had not had nearly enough time to find out what an unholy mess the previous administration had got this airport into. Once I did we revised our thinking and set a sensible schedule and we have stuck to it ever since.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The minister says that he discovered that things bogged down during the previous administration, but did it take him three years in which to discover that? Because after all when the criticism was directed toward him and toward his department this year and last year the present government had been in office two to three years respectively and nothing had been done.

The criticism which was levelled at the Department of Transport was in 1959. That is less than a year ago and the Montreal Gazette quoted the minister as saying the following.
In quotes?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
In quotes. Let me put it on
Hansard again:
Transport minister Hees led a troupe of M.P.s and department officials to the partially completed terminal at Montreal airport yesterday and said the new building would be ready next year-"as I always claimed it would be."
It is now 1960 and that is the minister's statement. I am not making this up; it is a direct quotation from the minister and I can send it over to him. So that if the position was as the minister claimed it was, it took him three years to discover it and to do something about it, and he did not get out of the bog until the criticism came from this side of the house.
I did not say that was the only reason. I know that another reason was due to the officers of his department who, faced with a critical situation not only at Montreal but at Uplands and Winnipeg and other airports, decided to bend every effort toward progress in construction of the airport. But there is no doubt that there was a tremendous bogging down so far as Montreal was concerned judging from the report the minister made, because here in the Gazette appears the statement:
Those who accompanied the official party-the minister, the deputy minister, the chief architect, the chief engineer-and the M.P.s on the tour were struck by the few workmen visible on any of the floors.
I could go on and read how disappointed the group was with the slow progress made at the airport. At that time the minister announced that the cost of the facilities had now reached $30 million, although as late as the previous year-that was 1958-the minister had said in the House of Commons that the cost would be $15 million.

As I said earlier, it took a few months to realize that this airport could not be completed until the end of 1960. That was obvious when I took the members on the tour of the airport in 1959. There is no statement that I made at that time, of which I am aware, which indicated anything but that the airport would be finished by the end of 1960. I have never yet claimed that I have been misquoted. I simply say that I have no recollection of ever saying it would be finished earlier, because it was never in my mind at any time that the airport could be completed before the end of 1960. There seems to have been some misunderstanding.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Perhaps the minister could be excused for thinking it had already been

completed, because on November 7, 1954 the previous minister, Mr. Marler, announced that it would be completed early in 1957, and I know that the hon. member for Laurier had previously announced that it would be built- I have not got my file with me at the moment but the hon. member could perhaps tell us the prediction he made at that time. When the present minister came to office he might well have thought the project was completed, since Liberal ministers always kept their promises.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Let me tell the hon. member now that when I made an announcement there was no statement as far as I can recollect, and I have to speak from memory now, in so far as a completion date was concerned. I think that goes for Mr. Marler, too, but again I may be mistaken. However, there were three definite statements here by the present minister as to the date of completion and still we are waiting in Montreal for the final opening which, I hope, will come in 1960.

Is the minister now in a position to say if tenders have actually been called for the terminal building at Sault Ste Marie? I am concerned because the appropriation for terminal buildings may be used up before tenders are called for the Soo.
They have not been called yet, but I can assure the hon. member for Algoma West that his airport will not be forgotten. We shall be calling for tenders later this year.

May I ask the minister one question pursuant to the starred questions which were asked today. I should like to know if the minister could say when it is expected that work will start on this new runway at Vancouver, and when it will be completed.
I believe work has actually started. If it has not, it will be started very soon and we expect completion next year.
The minister probably does not recall the number of work days that he gave today.

The number I quoted today was
200.

I wonder if the minister could tell me whether or not there is an amount entered this year to build a terminal and administration building for Yellowknife and replace that two by four chickencoop we are using their now.
It is not in the estimates this year, but I hope to get it into the estimates next year.

That is not what you people were telling the voters there in the campaigns of 1957 and 1958.

I think the hon. member asked that question earlier. I believe he indulges in the same practice as the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King who never asked a question unless he knew the answer first. I think the hon. member mentioned this date before. It was just before this government took over, and it was opened, as I think the hon. member also drew to the attention of the house, by Mr. St. Laurent.

It was opened by Mr. St.
Laurent. I just wanted to get this firmly on record because the minister, in one of those fits of exuberance earlier in the session, claimed this airport as one which had been built by the present administration, just as it is the practice of hon. gentlemen opposite to claim the credit for everything which was done and paid for out of Mr. Harris' last budget, as being done by them.
No, we just speeded it up and brought it to a satisfactory conclusion.
Certainly not Stephenville.

I thought the minister was making a joke, although he was not smiling, when he said that when the government gave an assurance they always stuck to it. I should like to direct his attention to the situation at Winnipeg airport. On August 30, 1958, as reported in Hansard on page 4369, the minister, in reply to a question I asked him about Winnipeg airfield plans, said:
We have worked our way through four different sets of plans to date, and we hope that we are working now on the final set of plans.
That was in 1958 in a discussion of the estimates at the stage we have reached now. In the following year the minister told us with respect to Winnipeg airfield, as reported in Hansard of June 12, on page 4666 that the vote contained $3 million for the Winnipeg air terminal. We know, of course, that practically no progress was made in spending that money in the fiscal year 1959-60.
Now the minister refers to another type of target, a target of final completion which he suggests will be in 1964. I do not need to tell the hon. gentleman that in the city of Winnipeg the administration has a newspaper which is normally very friendly to the Conservative government, but it does not think very much of the minister's target dates in so far as the airport at Winnipeg is concerned, because on June 4 of this year

Supply-Transport
an editorial which appeared in this friendly paper in Winnipeg commented as follows:
George Hees must think he is a medieval cathedral builder and that it does not matter whether the job is finished this century or next.
If Prime Minister Diefenbaker cannot persuade Mr. Hees and his department to give Winnipeg a modern airport building within two years he should fire the lot of them.
That, of course, is the comment of a friendly newspaper, and I suggest that the target date of 1964 is not one that is pleasing to the people of Winnipeg.

If the hon. member would read a little further back in those editorials he will And that the thing which got the people of Winnipeg really annoyed about this whole matter was that the former Liberal government began promising this airport in about 1944 and had promised it every year since then, so that by the time 1959 came along, after ten years of frustration, one can well understand their feeling of anxiety coupled with hope that at last a government had come into office which really would build them this fine terminal building. Of course they have found that this is the case, and now everybody is happy in Winnipeg.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is a great deal of discussion going on at I.C.A.O. in Montreal in connection with the various radio equipment for aircraft. I do not remember the technical terms that are used, but I am sure the minister has them or, if not, his officials will have them. Yes, Mr. Chairman. I have now had a chance to review the documentation relating to adoption by the council of I.C.A.O. of DME as a world-wide standard, and can add nothing to my previous statement of April 11 except that this does not, in any way, affect the continued implementation of the VOR program in Canada. 439. Administration, operation and maintenance. $229,050.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on this item I cannot resist putting on Hansard some of the choice expressions and statements employed by a number of the minister's colleagues when they sat on this side of the house. The committee will remember that in 1956 the Telegraphs Act was approved and adopted by parliament, known as chapter 49 of the Revised Statutes of 1956. It was very severely criticized by the then members of the opposition. I intend to read quickly a few of the expressions they employed on that occasion:
The aim of this measure is obviously the protection of another crown corporation against competition.
If this bill is passed in its present form, the only regard that needs to be had is at the caprice, if you will, of the order in council, regardless of the public interest.

The effect of those regulations, I think the minister will admit, would be to create a monopoly___We do not know who will be exercising the responsibilities under this legislation. I think it is not in the public interest. I think it is unfair to those who have been engaged in this business in the past.
Those statements were made when the bill was being considered in the committee of the whole house and may be found at pages 6736, 6744, 6749 and 6750 of Hansard of July 31, 1956. On third reading of the bill the following statements were made by the present Secretary of State for External Affairs as reported at pages 6755-56 of Hansard of that date:

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The official opposition are very much concerned about this bill because we believe a
step is being taken which is very unsound____We
have made our position clear. We think the government is making a great mistake.
On third reading the same opposition was expressed to the amendment to this act. But what happened? Lo and behold, quietly and unknown to anybody, this is what happened. There appeared in the Canada Gazette, part II, for Wednesday, March 9, 1960 at page 267 a proclamation of the Conservative government proclaiming the Telegraphs Act which was adopted by parliament in 1956. I am sorry the Minister of Justice is not here. He likes to place us in contradiction with statements we made when on the other side of the house. Where could there be any greater contradiction than that found in the statements made by the four ministers to whom I have referred when they spoke

against the bill to amend the Telegraphs Act which, when they were in office, they proclaimed?
Mr. Chairman, would the minister tell us what the present situation is with respect to telephone cables? Is the second telephone cable being laid?
The joint Canada-United Kingdom telephone cable is being laid and it is expected to be ready next year.
Has it got the same partnership arrangement as with the cable that was opened a few years ago?
No, Mr. Chairman, the first cable had a majority United Kingdom ownership. This is a Canada-United Kingdom partnership on an equal basis.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to remind the minister of something to which I have referred in the past. As I review the reference to federal responsibility in the matter of telephones and telegraphs it seems to be contained in a relatively short section of a very large act, the Railway Act. I think it is time that this should be looked at with the possibility in mind of having more clearly set out what is the federal responsibility with respect to the control and regulation of telephones. It has been my experience that where there is a possibility of a clash between an independent telephone company that may have its jurisdiction with the province on the one hand and a federally incorporated telephone company on the other there is a great deal of uncertainty and havoc in the area concerned. You sometimes have two people trying to operate in the same area. It is my view that a revision of the legislation is required. Consideration should be given to the suggestion that under certain conditions telephone companies can receive some direction and control and regulation from the board of transport commissioners although frequently the board says their only concern is with a federally incorporated company. I believe this requires review.

Mr. Chairman, one question occurred to me as I was reflecting on those interesting quotations which were read by the hon. member for Laurier. Is the minister at all troubled that the amendments to the Telegraphs Act which he shared the responsibility for proclaiming will come into conflict with the bill of rights?

No, Mr. Chairman, it just shows that when a party which for many years has been denied vital information from a government which refused for years to give it acquires that information when it forms the
Supply-Transport
government then it can carry on in a much more enlightened way and bring in good legislation like this government has done for the past three years.
In other words, the minister is saying that he did not understand the bill when he spoke against it?
On the contrary, Mr. Chairman, I understood the bill as well as I could on the basis of the very limited information imparted to us by the previous minister.

441. Administration, operation and maintenance including Canada's assessment for membership in the world meteorological organization, $15,210,370.

Mr. Chairman, has the minister been able to come any closer to supplying the requested assignment of meteorologists to the forest fire forecasting service in British Columbia? Perhaps the minister is aware that we are now being plagued by various serious forest fires there. For several years there has been a request for an assignment for meteorologists for this service. I notice there is quite an increase in the vote and I wonder if the minister has any information concerning whether the department can make that assignment?

No, Mr. Chairman, we are still short of meteorologists. We will not be able to do what the hon. member wishes until our recruiting program has been completed. We will carry it out as quickly as possible but we do not expect it will be possible to meet that request until next year.

Mr. Chairman, can the minister say anything encouraging about the recruiting program? Does he still have to go outside the country to recruit meteorologists or has the pay been increased to the point that would make it an attractive occupation for Canadians?
The main trouble has been the salary scale. That question is before treasury board at the present moment and I am very hopeful that it will be satisfactorily resolved in the very near future.
Is the department still recruiting outside the country?
Only if it is impossible to find meteorologists in Canada. We have recruited a small number from outside the country.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask if the headquarters of the meteorological service are still at the University of Toronto?

Yes, and likely to remain so, Mr. Chairman.

Supply-Transport

I have a question I should like to raise with the minister under this vote. I have had extensive correspondence over a couple of years with the office in Toronto, which I understand is the head office of this branch. I forget the name of the individual with whom I was corresponding. It seems to me he was the chief or director of that branch. In any event it had to do with the weather forecasts given for the north coastal region of British Columbia. Unfortunately, Kitimat and Terrace are lumped in with either Prince Rupert, the north coast forecast, or with Smithers and the interior forecast. Up until the time that Kitimat started to become a large industrial centre there probably was not too much desire or pressure to have that area localized in the weather forecast. But there are some 10,000 to 12,000 people in that area and unfortunately the residents of Kitimat are not sure into which weather forecast they fall. I think they would fall properly into the weather forecast of the north coastal area, Prince Rupert and so on, because it is on the coast. I have been unsuccessful in dealing with this matter by correspondence with the director, or the chap in Toronto whose name escapes me, and I make a plea to the minister to have this area set apart as a separate area for weather forecasts so that the people will know when the weather forecast does come just which forecast applies to them. Whether or not the forecast is correct is another matter and can be dealt with at another time. I am merely talking about pinpointing it in so far as the weather forecast is concerned.

I am advised that the regional approach is all we can handle unless we double or triple or staff, although the request made by the hon. member is a reasonable one. We are limited at the present time by these considerations but I will agree that what he asks for is a desirable thing and we shall certainly keep that in mind as we are able to enlarge this operation.

I do not think the physical inability to do this at the present time has anything to do with enlarging the staff. I had occasion to check statistical material on this when we were dealing with the Postmaster General and facilities in Kitimat. According to the climate statistics, Kitimat is in substantially the same position as Prince Rupert, and the weather forecast that would apply to Prince Rupert generally would apply to Kitimat. Both places are on the coast; both are on salt water, both have the same sort of wind conditions. The British Columbia department of agriculture does take weather samples and surveys in that area; that is, the amount of rainfall, precipitation,

sunshine and that sort of thing. I think all that would be necessary would be for the weather forecast just to mention the Kitimat and Terrace areas. I think the minister will find on investigation that it will be almost the same type of forecast that would apply to the Prince Rupert coastal area. That is all we are asking.
Mr. Chairman, we shall certainly look into the possibilities of doing what the hon. member asks.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have just one question. Is there any new development by way of equipment in the field of meteorological services?
Yes; I am advised that many new instruments have been devised that are constantly changing the techniques, but it would be quite an operation; I am afraid I could not go into the details now.

I have had a number of requests to have a weather forecast station set up in southern Saskatchewan. We find that we are now depending on weather forecasts from quite some distance away and owing to the complex and intricate nature of our farming operations-I am thinking now of flax cultivation-the farmers have been somewhat inconvenienced by the daily inaccurate forecasts they receive. Once the minister has the increase in staff he speaks of I should like to see this matter considered and have a weather forecast station in southern Saskatchewan.
I shall be glad to give that consideration, Mr. Chairman.
When the hon. member gets that station I hope he will get better results than he got from the political forecast in Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Is there any way that we can get better forecasting for the general public? I read the ones that are posted every day in the elevators, and I think we get better results from "Chase's Almanac" on many occasions. The fronts that are given are so broad that they do not take local situations into consideration. If the type of report that is given to each one of the areas is the type that we get on the radio stations on a daily basis I can see very little value in them. I am particularly concerned with our lake and the fact that many of our people are going to have to depend more and more on these weather reports not only for planting crops but also for safety measures. It is a large lake and it gets very rough. Instead of there being only two and three large boats on it there are hundreds and hundreds of very small ones. I imagine this situation is

repeated all across the country. It information is to be given on the local radio station, then it must be a lot better than the general forecasts that we see. If it is not it is of no value. I say that because we have extensive facilities all across the country. We spend a lot of money maintaining these stations throughout the north and all over Canada. We should have a much better understanding of what the weather is going to be. I refer not only to long range forecasts of four or five days but particularly the short range forecasts. If we are going to go out into the country for a day we should know what weather conditions we are going to run into. We should be able to have a forecast a couple of days previously. If there is not this type of clear-cut forecasting, then I wonder whether something cannot be done to obtain that type of forecast?

I quite agree with the hon. member that inaccurate weather forecasts are very disturbing indeed. However, I hasten to tell him that weather forecasting still is not an exact science. We are doing our best to improve all along the line and to make those forecasts as accurate as possible. I again state that forecasting is not an exact science; we are doing our best to make it so.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I should like to mention the boating accident last night on the Ottawa river. I would assume that a yacht club the size of the Britannia yacht club would probably follow the weather reports very closely and should have some method of warning that a squall is coming up. I would think it was not a completely localized squall; it must have blown in from somewhere. That type of information should be available to prevent calamities from happening.
I am advised that it was a very localized squall and occurred in only a very limited area.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to say a word of praise of the weather forecasts. I know that when I am in my constituency I always blame the weather on the minister but, in fact, the weather is not under the control of the government. I do believe that the meteorological service does a wonderful job, and that the forecasts over the radio are of enormous help to a considerable number of people. Anyone who spends time, and wishes he was spending it right now, on the Atlantic coast, appreciates how valuable these weather forecasts are.
I appreciate very much those kind words.
